Name: 0% overdue invoices, 99% of the time: How Nourished Accounting gets paid on time, (almost) every time
Post Body:
“It's not malicious. People aren't trying to not pay you. They're just busy people or busy business owners. And the easier that you can make it for them, the quicker you'll get the cash.”‍

Emily Vass started Nourished Accounting to help small business owners feel confident about their numbers. She saw how often finance was avoided - not because people didn’t care, but because it felt overwhelming or unclear. With a focus on education, Emily uses social content and client work to simplify complex topics.

Emily started using Adfin when she was still a sole trader, putting the right payment structure in place early. As her business grew and moved to a limited company, that setup stayed with her. Today, the firm’s overdue invoice rate is nearly always 0%. Emily is realistic: occasionally a client pays late - but when that happens, having a system that means you can resolve it quickly makes all the difference.

A lean tech stack

Emily’s approach to technology has always been measured: start lean, and only introduce tools when they genuinely reduce friction.

The firm now runs on:

  • Xero for bookkeeping and recurring invoices
  • Engager for engagement letters and practice management
  • Adfin, connected to both, to handle payments and credit control

The key requirement is that everything integrates. Payment isn’t treated as a separate administrative task - it sits inside the wider workflow.

The key element: payments as part of onboarding

As Nourished began taking on more clients, Emily knew onboarding needed to be clear and consistent. Moving someone from discovery call to active client should feel straightforward - both for the team and for the client. When Adfin integrated with Engager, it solved a practical problem: instead of managing engagement letters in one place and payment setup somewhere else, the two could sit within the same flow.

Now, when a client agrees to work with Nourished, they sign their engagement letter and set up their direct debit as part of that process. For clients on monthly packages, Xero recurring invoices run automatically, and Adfin collects in the background. Emily rarely needs to step in unless a package or price changes.

‍

Keeping overdue close to zero

Nourished’s overdue rate is nearly always at 0%. Emily is careful not to present that as perfection - sometimes clients do pay late, but the difference is that those invoices don’t linger.

Two factors make that possible:

Clear boundaries from the outset

For example, with tax returns, the process is consistent:

  • The draft return is prepared
  • The invoice is issued
  • Submission follows once payment has been received

Because expectations are set early, it rarely results in difficult conversations. Clients know that once payment is made, their return is filed promptly. The firm holds up its side of the agreement just as clearly.

Tools that resolve issues quickly

On the rare occasion an invoice goes overdue, the aim is to resolve it efficiently rather than escalate it. Adfin gives Emily the tools to resolve it quickly:

  • Visibility over invoice status
  • WhatsApp reminders
  • Quick payment links

 In practice, a well-timed message with an easy way to pay is often enough.

Results

By connecting onboarding, recurring billing and credit control into one joined-up workflow with Adfin and Engager, Nourished Accounting has achieved:

  • An overdue invoice rate that is nearly always 0%
  • Fast resolution when something does slip
  • Monthly billing that runs automatically in the background

Emily’s set up means she gets paid on time, (almost) every time. If overdue invoices are becoming a problem, speak to our team about how Adfin can help bring them down.

Name: 4 ways to improve your account receivable and get paid faster
Post Body:
Getting paid for a job well done is satisfying. At the same time, chasing down late payments is one of the most frustrating things that firms face on a regular when managing their accounts receivable collections.

If it feels like your firm is always chasing after clients it might be a red flag that there’s something off in your accounts receivable (AR) processes. In the world of finance, understanding the ar meaning in business is crucial for maintaining a healthy cash flow.

But don’t despair! We’ve seen many firms face this realisation. Truly solving your accounts receivable invoice issues involves taking an honest look at what you’re doing currently and identifying areas where you can increase efficiency and be more cost-effective. And while getting paid on time has likely been a challenge for as long as money has existed, fortunately for us, we have modern accounts receivable automation software to help us solve these problems. 

‍

The true cost of inefficient processes

There are many reasons why late payments hurt businesses. Late payments threaten cash flow and drain valuable time and resources.. 

Frequent late payments can cause tension in client relationships, are a financial and operational burden, and hurt morale for the employees tasked with chasing those payments. This is where an effective accounts receivable system can make a significant difference.

‍

The hidden costs of manual processes

Manual processes are slow, tedious, and error-prone, making them a silent killer in accounts receivable management.  All that time spent manually chasing invoices adds up, as 31% of businesses spend 21 to 30 hours per month chasing overdue invoices–with 55% of those businesses seeing an increasing number of late payments. 

Manual collections mean a higher risk of mistakes, lost productivity, and more stress but you don’t have to watch as your day sales outstanding (DSO) gets longer and longer. Implementing ar automation can significantly streamline your billing procedures and improve collection effectiveness.

So let’s explore how to improve your processes so you get paid within days instead of weeks or months, optimizing your cash flow and enhancing your revenue forecast.

‍

4 ways to improve your process

Here are some tips to turn your manual accounts receivable process into a well-oiled machine:

1. Automated reminders 🔔

Stop chasing after clients and sending endless manual follow-ups. With platforms like Adfin, an advanced AR software, you can automate your invoice and reminder workflows and cross those manual reminders off your to-do list permanently. This ar automation feature allows for customizable follow-ups, ensuring a consistent and professional approach to collections.

‍

2. Incentives and penalties AKA the carrot and stick ✅❌

Enforcing prompt payment discounts and late penalties can be very effective tools to nudge payers in the right direction - but billers have traditionally been put off by the additional admin required to make sure everything reconciles in their accounting software. Some billers are also worried about harming client relationships if they enforce late penalties.

As long as you clearly state your payment terms on your original invoice, and stay within the law, you are quite within your rights to enforce late payment penalties. Having a third party like Adfin administer those fees can also help preserve your client relationships while improving your accounts receivable collections..

And prompt payment incentives are particularly beneficial for the clients who may forget to make manual transfers for weeks on end. This approach can significantly improve your invoice strategy and reduce credit risk.

‍

3. Flexible options 🧘

If you want to get paid faster, it makes sense to make paying as easy as possible for clients. That includes being flexible by providing different payment options such as credit cards, direct debit, and open banking. This approach to payment processing enhances the overall customer payment experience.

This is a great move because it’s more convenient, enhances the payment experience for clients, and it can even be a competitive advantage compared to less flexible firms. By offering various online payments options and payment portals, you're making it easier for clients to pay, which can significantly reduce your days sales outstanding.

‍

4. Lower fees = lower costs 📉

Hidden fees and high fees are consistent challenges for many businesses–and the only thing worse is fees that are both! This is where efficient accounts receivable solutions can make a significant difference.

This year alone, the total value of B2B payment transactions in the UK is $2.8 trillion. Different payment platforms and merchants charge different fees, but even a 1% fee would equal $28 billion!

In the previous section, we talked about the importance of offering different payment options so it’s as easy as possible for clients to pay. But those different payment platforms and merchants all charge different types of fees. Some charge a flat fee per transaction while others charge a percentage (usually between 1 - 2.5%).

Managing these different payment options can be a headache: multiple sources of truth to reconcile and multiple vendors to manage, all with their own fee structures. This is where an integrated accounts receivable system can help streamline your processes and reduce costs.

Name: 5 tips for credit control that get you paid faster
Post Body:
Adfin is the ‘Just Get Paid’ company for a reason. What should be simple for small businesses - getting paid for the goods/services they deliver - is still not straightforward. 

The numbers back this up - research from FreeAgent showed that almost two-thirds of invoices sent by UK small firms were paid late in the past year, and Sage estimated that £112 billion of UK cash flow is currently locked up in late payments. 

This means having a strong credit control process that gets you paid on time is critical, and could be the difference between smooth cashflow and missing monthly payroll. 

We’ve broken down the key steps to building a great credit control process below. 

1. A single source of truth for your receivables

Having a single view of all receivables in one place is an absolute must-have. You need to be able to assess what’s due, what’s late and what needs chasing. 

At Adfin, we’ve built a credit control dashboard that shows all your invoices and payments, synced in real time with your accounting software. We’ve made it fully flexible, so you can group by credit control status or action required, sort and filter by any field, and choose exactly what data you want to see, so you can act upon them. 

2. Good quality customer data

Once you know which invoices you need to chase, the next step is making sure you’ve got the right people to follow up with. Bounced email addresses, outdated phone numbers or missing contact information can all delay collections. 

Adfin surfaces this information for you automatically. If an email bounces or a phone number is incorrect, you’ll see it straight away in the Adfin Console. That means you can act quickly to update the right information and keep the collections process moving along. 

3. Quick and consistent follow ups

Following up promptly when invoices are due is one of the simplest ways to improve your payment times. Most late payments aren’t intentional - people forget, emails get missed, and priorities change, so giving them a gentle reminder should be your first port of call. 

Defining a process you can stick to makes this easier; a reminder on the due date, another a few days after, then a clear escalation if needed. Keeping the tone friendly and confident helps maintain good customer relationships while still getting results.

The challenge here can be carving time out of a busy work day for this - copying and pasting invoice information into emails isn’t a good use of time for anyone. 

We found this ourselves at Adfin, and built Autopilot to fix this. Autopilot sends reminders for you, in your own tone of voice and from your own email domain. It automatically fills out the relevant customer information like amount owed and due date, and you can check and review emails before they are sent. In short, Autopilot saves you time from the mundane bits, but still gives you control to keep your customer interactions authentic.  

4. Learn what works for your customers (and something is better than nothing!)

We’ve all been there - you’ve chased a customer countless times, only for them to come back to you and ask to pay another way, or delay a payment because they need more time.

This is where having the right mix of payment options comes in. With Adfin, you can choose between direct debit for recurring payments, instalment plans to help customers spread large invoices over time, and Apple / Google Pay to make it easy to pay in one tap from a phone. 

We’ve just launched partial payments, which let customers pay what they can upfront while you collect the remaining balance later. You can set a minimum amount, so you stay in control while still giving customers flexibility when they need it.

You can also customise your chasing workflows by customer with Adfin. The customer that always pays on time - no reminders needed. The one that always needs chasing - an automated Whatsapp reminder every 3 days with the payment link embedded. 

So with Adfin you’ve got a personalised process for each of your customers, with no additional legwork for you. 

5. Track results over time 

Lastly, a good credit control process is not just about today’s overdue invoices - it’s about spotting patterns. Are certain customers always late? Are your outstanding receivables trending in the right direction? 

In Adfin, you can see this at a glance. Your dashboard shows unpaid vs received amounts for this month and last month, so you can instantly check how you’re doing and whether your credit control process is working.

Name: Accountants and Bookkeepers, top 5 strategies to improve your cash flow
Post Body:
As an accountant or bookkeeper, managing your own business cash flow is crucial. Just like your clients, you need to ensure a steady cash flow management to keep your business running smoothly. Implementing accounts receivable automation tools and effective credit control processes can significantly improve your financial health. Here are top 5 cash flow strategies you can use to improve your cash flow forecasting, reduce administrative burdens, and focus more on growing your practice.

1. Automate your invoicing process

One of the simplest ways to improve your cash flow is to implement an automated invoicing process. By utilizing an invoice management solution, you can ensure that invoices are sent out in a timely manner and are received in a way that is clear and straightforward for the payer - using their preferred channels: whether it’s email, SMS, or Whatsapp.

This leads to faster payments and a more consistent cash flow. Implementing automated invoicing is a key part of a robust credit control process, ensuring that all invoices are tracked and managed efficiently.

2. Implement intelligent payment reminders

Chasing down payments is one of the most frustrating aspects of managing accounts receivable, consuming significant time and resources. Implementing intelligent invoice reminders, beyond what’s typically included in accounting softwares, can significantly reduce the time spent on this task.

An advanced accounts receivable platform can automatically send out smart reminders to clients before payments are due. These invoice reminders can be customized using AI to adjust the tone based on the payer, context, and time of day, ensuring your clients are prompted to pay on time without feeling harassed. This results in faster and more consistent payments.

Incorporating intelligent payment smart reminders automates your credit control process, helping you maintain a steady cash flow and reducing overdue payments.

3. Offer multiple payment options

Making it easy for your clients to pay you is key to improving your cash flow. Offering multiple payment options, such as Direct Debits, credit cards, and bank transfers, gives your clients the flexibility to choose the payment method that works best for them. Implementing electronic payment systems and customer payment portals can further enhance this flexibility.

When clients have more options to pay, they are more likely to settle their invoices promptly. An advanced accounts receivable platform can integrate various payment methods, making the payment process seamless for your clients and ensuring that you get paid faster. Consider implementing payment scheduling options to allow clients to set up future payments, further streamlining payment processes.

4. Implement “early payment” discounts and “late payment” fees

Incentivizing your clients to pay early can be a highly effective strategy to improve your cash flow. Offering early payment discounts encourages clients to pay their invoices ahead of time, providing you with the funds you need sooner.

Alternatively, implementing late payment fees can discourage clients from delaying their payments. While you don’t want to penalize your clients harshly, a small late fee can serve as a reminder for them to pay on time. This combination of rewards and penalties can help you maintain a steady cash flow. Using early payment discounts and late payment fees as part of your credit control process ensures timely payments and minimizes overdue accounts, contributing to effective late payment prevention.

5. Integrate with accounting software

You can't manage what you don't measure. Having everything synced back to your accounting software through accounting software integration allows you to understand your cash flow position clearly and identify areas (e.g customers, invoices, services) where you can double down to improve it. Using an accounts receivable platform that areis integrated with your accounting software ensures that all your invoicing, payment reminders, and payment collections are automatically updated in real-time. 

With this financial workflow automation, you can easily track your cash flow, monitor outstanding invoices, and generate real-time financial reports. This visibility enables you to make informed decisions about your business, ensuring you stay on top of your cash flow and improve your financial situation.

Conclusion

Implementing the following strategies can significantly improve your cash flow strategies can significantly improve your accounts receivable optimization:

  1. Automate your invoicing process.
  2. Implement intelligent payment reminders.
  3. Offer multiple payment options.
  4. Leverage early payment discounts and late payment fees.
  5. Integrate with your accounting software.

These strategies help you establish a comprehensive credit control process, ensuring a steady cash flow management while freeing up your time to focus on growing your practice. By incorporating these simple yet effective methods, you can greatly enhance the financial health of your business through improved accounts receivable automation.

Start implementing these strategies today and experience the positive impact they can have on your business cash flow and overall business operations.

Name: Adfin emerges from stealth with $4.9m (€4.5m) in funding to build the best way for bills to get paid
Post Body:
We launched Adfin because we believe there’s a better way for consumers and businesses to manage payments. Now, we’re joined in that mission by co-lead investors Index Ventures and Visionaries Club, along with a prominent set of angels, including Guillaume Pousaz (Checkout.com founder), Thijn Lamers (Adyen founding team), Josef Bovet, (Tiller co-founder), Maximilian Eber and Maik Wehmeyer (Taktile founders), David de Picciotto (Pledge co-founder), Ferdinand Meyer (Moss co-founder), and Eugene Danilkis (Mambu co-founder).

‍

The decades of fintech experience we have between us have exposed the shortcomings of open banking and the limitations of modern billing products. Open banking can be low-cost, but it’s simply not ready for everyone. Bill payments are still painfully manual for senders and payers. That’s why we’re on a mission to fix bill payments for everyone with Adfin. Combining state-of-the-art payment technologies with AI-powered insights, we’re providing the most seamless, fast and cost-effective experience for businesses and consumers alike. 

‍

Bill payments are stuck in the 1990s

‍

European fintech entrepreneurs have transformed how money is moved since the 2010s, but somehow billing was left conspicuously untouched. As a result, processing and paying bills remains a horrible experience on both sides. For the most part, businesses are stuck with convincing customers to set up a direct debit, managing the arduous process of having them send a bank transfer, or settling for taking card payments – with the accompanying fees. For smaller businesses like tradespeople and lawyers, significant resources and time is spent chasing payments. Often they will resort to processing cards over the phone. This creates an extra burden for their bookkeepers, who are left piecing together transactions from a patchwork of antiquated sources. 

‍

For payers, things aren’t any better. Payments mean inputting lines of address, entering card numbers or account details, and triple checking that everything is correct so that the payment doesn’t fail – or, worse, is sent to the wrong place. Fraudsters are taking advantage of the confusion by impersonating billers, stealing people’s house deposits or clearing out their accounts. These bad experiences for payers translate to bad outcomes for billers, who struggle with cashflow simply because people can’t face the stress-inducing payment process.

‍

Open banking isn’t all it’s cracked up to be

‍

Open banking was meant to at least reduce payment costs for companies through instant transfers between any account. But consumer adoption has been slow – in the UK, just 11% of the public use the system, compared to 17% of businesses. Only around 50% of the UK population use the mobile banking apps necessary in the first place to make open banking a good experience. 

‍

No biller – even the largest – can be expected to stay on top of the ever-changing payment mix, but being behind the curve can cost them a meaningful percentage of revenue. At Adfin, we solve this by intelligently combining best-in-class open banking technology with card payments. Using our AI-powered system means that each time, not only the fastest and cheapest payment option for the business is used, but the one that will maximise the likelihood of a successful payment based on individual payer insights. This product is unique in Europe and possibly worldwide.

‍

No one tool was perfect for the job. That’s why we’re building Adfin

‍

As infrastructure experts, we saw first-hand how no one tool was perfect for the job. We wanted to make best-in-class payments accessible to everyone. Our first product is squarely focused on solving the problem of getting invoices paid for businesses in the fastest, cheapest and most effective way possible:

‍

  • Small business owners get their evenings back with Adfin. Say goodbye to the tedious tasks of generating and chasing invoices and bill payments. 
  • Bookkeepers can use Adfin to automate business or consumer invoice-to-cash processes, simply syncing all transitions to leading accountancy software without a single line of code needed. 
  • SaaS platforms integrate with Adfin to offer a seamless billing experience to business customers. Current implementation partners include legal practice management software SOS Legal and dental platform 32Co.
  • Bill payers use Adfin for a stress-free bill-paying experience, which strips away the layers of admin often associated with the process. 

‍

Assembling a team of fintech nerds to change billing

‍

We’re at the start of our journey, building a lean, high-impact team of fintech experts. We draw on decades of experience building fintechs in Europe, including open banking platform Tink and cloud banking platform Mambu, and have a roster of investors who have scaled some of Europe’s greatest fintech success stories. Get in touch if you want to join our journey and advance the state of the art in billing!

‍

Name: Adfin releases beta MCP server for AI clients
Post Body:
We believe finance is riddled with inefficient, manual processes. We combine payments infrastructure innovation with agentic AI to transform the financial operations of SMBs.

We always want to always make sure we’re on the leading edge of technology. Recently we hosted a hackathon to tackle a fundamental challenge in AI-driven fintech. Our goal? To develop an interface that allows you to use Adfin, from anywhere, anytime - via an LLM (large language model eg. Claude).

‍

For anyone unfamiliar with the concept of MCP (Model Context Protocol), here’s a quick introduction:

MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how applications provide context to LLMs. Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications. Just as USB-C provides a standardized way to connect your devices to various peripherals and accessories, MCP provides a standardized way to connect AI models to different data sources and tools. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction)

‍

Our idea was, if we can build an MCP Server - an Adfin customer can essentially talk to Adfin, from any LLM that supports MCP (eg. Claude desktop) - and have a new, decoupled, interface for managing all of their cashflow.

What we've built

We’ve released an MCP server that allows use of Claude desktop for almost all of the operations in the Adfin platform.

‍Here’s some examples:

🚀 Ask Claude about your Credit control, such as outstanding invoices (new APIs!).

🚀 Ask Claude to create you new customers in Adfin.

🚀 Ask Claude to create an invoice via text, send it to Adfin and activate reminders for it.

🚀 Upload an invoice to Claude, send it to Adfin and activate it.

🚀 Ask Claude to check the state of your invoices.

‍

‍

You can check out the MCP server here: https://github.com/Adfin-Engineering/mcp-server-adfin.

We have also published a video demonstration for anyone who just wants to see how it works, without the technical setup.

Interested in giving this a go, but don't know where to start? Shortly we will release some content around how to get this going on your own machine.

‍

Challenges

It wouldn’t be fair to highlight some of the challenges we’ve had with getting started with the MCP, so we’ve included some details on this. While most of this is down to the maturity of the MCP protocol, it shows that we still have some way to go before MCP can be mainstream.

‍

❌ Challenge 1: Lack of native oAuth:

Despite all the fun tools, the big limiting factor across for us, was the lack of native interface MCP for oAuth (which Adfin’s API relies upon, by design). Adfin’s APIs are predominantly driven by user level access, driven by user bearer tokens. There doesn’t seem to be a repeatable way to implement this today.

❌ Challenge 2: Protocol limitations

While we were able to successfully connect to the Adfin MCP server from the console, the value of such a server comes from an LLM having access to the tools to use as they see fit. However, the current limitations of the MCP protocol around authentication don't allow this, and also the output presented by the LLM to the user seems to be aimed at people with a technical background.

❌ Challenge 3: Spring framework limited our bridge between stdio and http.

A bridge was required for interoperability with Claude Sonnet Desktop app, which only supports stdio (for now). Unfortunately we were unable to make any of them work, it is not clear what is the issue. Could be either the bridge, either something on the spring boot MCP server, but we weren’t able to pinpoint the cause exactly. Eventually ditched the bridge as we changed strategy on how we integrate with Adfin APIs.

‍

Our conclusion

Despite encountering challenges, our journey into integrating the MCP protocol with Adfin's powerful payment infrastructure and AI capabilities has been incredibly exciting. The current limitations—particularly around authentication and infrastructure compatibility—highlight the early-stage nature of MCP, yet also underscore the immense potential this technology holds.

We're committed to continuing our exploration and innovation in this space. As MCP matures and evolves, we eagerly anticipate addressing these initial hurdles and unlocking even greater possibilities. Our experience thus far reinforces our belief in the transformative potential of standardized, context-aware interfaces in fintech.

We look forward to actively contributing to, and participating in, the future developments of MCP, ensuring that Adfin remains at the forefront of AI-driven financial innovation.

TL;DR: It’s very cool. Like really really cool. But it’s not quite as quick to get going as X/Twitter/LinkedIn would have you believe.

Name: Adfin’s integration with Xero saves on average 3 hours per week
Post Body:
Collecting a payment isn’t a single action, it’s a chain of steps across multiple systems. Customer details, invoices, email or SMS delivery, banks, payment networks, payment providers, payouts, accounting systems… and that’s before you even get to reconciliation.

When these systems don’t talk to each other properly (which is most of the time), the result is familiar:

  • poor payment experience
  • late payments
  • hours lost to manual reconciliation and troubleshooting

A classic example:

A customer pays by bank transfer, but the reference doesn’t match. The money’s in your bank, but Xero can’t reconcile it automatically. You’re now manually matching transactions, updating invoice statuses, and emailing customers to confirm payment.

That’s 30 minutes lost on a single payment.

The real problem: broken connections

From the early days of Adfin, we've spent most of our time talking to our users - especially accountants and bookkeepers. The scale of inefficiency in managing invoices and payments became immediately clear, particularly in reconciliations.

With Adfin, businesses don't need to worry about any of these. Adfin has built state-of-the-art integrations with each of these components, especially with Xero. We've invested years of development work and integrated feedback from thousands of accountants and bookkeepers to create the best Xero integration in the payments market (that’s what our users tell us, at least!).

There are four key characteristics that truly blow the mind of our users:

  1. Two-way sync - Changes made in either system are reflected in the other. Always.
  2. Real time - Updates appear in Adfin and Xero within seconds, not hours, not “eventually”.
  3. Complete - Most integrations handle the happy path. Adfin goes further and covers the edge cases that actually cause problems. That’s where the real time savings come from.
  4. Reliable - Built to run 24/7. When something needs attention, users are notified immediately

Below is a detailed breakdown of what the Adfin <> Xero integration does and why our users save tens of hours every month. 

Fully automated integration setup

The integration setup process is fully automated and it usually takes our users no more than a couple of minutes to connect Adfin to Xero - which includes setting up how invoices are captured, how payments are reconciled, bank and payouts configurations, importing and syncing customers. 

The result is totally worth it: two of the most business critical systems are properly wired to cover all those edge use cases and Adfin is added as a payment method in Xero, allowing businesses to Just Get Paid faster and cheaper than ever.

Adfin captures invoices from Xero

Adfin gives users full control on which invoices should be imported from Xero or just import all of them. Users that opt for granular control make use of branding themes to select whether Adfin should import the invoice and how it should be collected - via Auto Collect (Direct debit) or On Demand (card, Apple Pay, Google Pay, bank transfer).

Adfin captures the invoice, customer details, and line items, attaches the original Xero invoice PDF, and sends a payment request to the customer. The invoice is automatically marked as sent in Xero.

The part that our users love the most: once the invoice is linked, any update made in Xero is automatically reflected in Adfin, ensuring the correct amount is always collected and customers always see the latest invoice.

Adfin sends the invoices

Adfin ensures customers receive the invoices on their preferred communication channels - via email, WhatsApp or SMS text messages. For example, we’ve seen plenty of customers pay in seconds when the invoice is sent via WhatsApp and they click on the link and pay with Apple Pay.

Collecting payments using direct debit (Auto Collect)? Adfin handles the entire communication process:

  • No mandate yet? Adfin sends the invoice with a mandate request and starts collection automatically once signed.

  • Mandate already in place? Adfin sends the invoice for records and issues payment notices in line with BACS requirements.

The part that our users love the most: As with everything in Adfin, all of these flows are fully configurable, including selecting communication channels, mandate chasing frequencies, whether to send invoices right away or later etc.

Adfin sends reminders automatically

Adfin’s credit control automation follows up on unpaid invoices via email, WhatsApp, and SMS. Users control when, how, and how often reminders are sent.

The part that our users love the most: Adfin Autopilot - the AI-powered tool that sends personalised reminders to the customer based on the business tone of voice, adapted to the context of each customer. It keeps good customers happy - and gets difficult payers to pay faster.

Adfin collects the payment and reconciles instantly

Adfin supports all major payment methods in one place:

  • Direct debit
  • Card
  • Apple Pay & Google Pay
  • Bank transfer
  • Open Banking

This means consistent reconciliation in Xero, reducing manual reconciliation efforts and making it easier to understand what’s going on.

Adfin creates the payment on the invoice in Xero right away after the customer has paid and posts the transaction on the Adfin clearing bank account. If payment is reverted for some reason (like a failed direct debit), Adfin automatically reverts the payment in Xero and continues the payment collection process with automated retries and fallbacks to card payments.

The part that our users love the most: Sometimes, customers just pay differently - in cash, via a cheque or directly into your bank account. Adfin syncs all these manual payments that are logged in Xero, making sure that invoice amounts are reduced by any partial payments or chasing stops when the invoice is fully paid (or voided) in Xero. 

Double the love: Sometimes, these manually posted payments in Xero are reverted - Adfin covers for that as well, by automatically cancelling the payment and resuming collection with the new amount.

Adfin automatically syncs credit notes

Adfin syncs all credit notes from Xero. When a credit note is applied on an invoice, Adfin will reduce the collection amount.

Edit the credit note amount or delete the credit note? Adfin will immediately read the change and update the collection amount.

Fast payouts, fully reconciled

We know how important cash is for businesses, so unlike many providers, Adfin doesn’t sit on your funds. We execute the payout as soon as the money is available. All the payouts are automatically reconciled in Xero between the Adfin clearing account and the business bank account.

Adfin collects and reconciles payment links (payments without an invoice)

Adfin has a complete integration with Xero for managing payments without an invoice as well - like payment links or direct debit payment schedules.

Each business has its own way of handling these payments. Therefore, Adfin offers 3 ways of managing these payments in Xero: as a receive money transaction, as an overpayment users can easily apply on the invoices directly in Xero, or as a prepayment, which allows automatically reconciling VAT as well.

Adfin keeps the users informed

Users get full visibility on the data that’s synced between Adfin and Xero. The activity feed in Adfin at invoice and customer level shows the updates that were made to or from Xero and their status.

Whenever there is an issue in Xero, it will be highlighted in the activity feed. Whenever there is an impediment processing the update in Adfin, Adfin will inform the users via email or in-app notifications.

Users can rest assured that Adfin will let them know when their attention or manual intervention is required. 

  • Xero and Adfin disconnected? Adfin will send an email and show a banner in the app, so users can take action. 
  • Payment cannot be synced to Xero due the accounting period being closed? Adfin will send users an email notification.
  • Customer was deleted in Xero while their invoice was still under collection in Adfin? Adfin will email the user telling them how to fix the issue.

Customer records, always in sync

Users can import customers from Xero to Adfin either as a mass import of all customers or filtered by specific Xero customer groups. Users can then decide if new customers assigned to the customer group in Xero should be auto-imported in Adfin.

Adfin then keeps the customer records in sync:

  • When an invoice is captured in Adfin from Xero, Adfin automatically reads the customer details.
  • When the customer's details are changed in Xero, Adfin applies the updates. The same happens in reverse: Xero is updated when customers are changed in Adfin.

The part that our users love the most: Adfin can send notifications to multiple contacts at the same time, so the right customers get the payment request or the reminder. This feature also enables invoices to be pushed to bookkeeping tools for automated reconciliation.

Built for accountants. Loved by businesses.

These are the top reasons why our users and thousands of accountants love the Adfin <> Xero integration. And our investment in this integration is ongoing, expanding to cover more use cases in our mission to fully automate everything payments for our users.

Name: Announcing our October Release
Post Body:
Adfin unveils full revenue automation for client-first businesses 

Adfin, the leading revenue operations platform for client-first businesses, now allows SMBs to fully automate revenue collection end to end for the first time with a host of new features: including the world’s first end-to-end agentic AI chasing tool, Adfin Autopilot.

Putting credit control on Autopilot 

For many businesses, getting paid is still a struggle. As a result, many SMBs now have a dedicated credit control function within their business that takes care of manually chasing for payment: checking who’s paid, drafting and sending personalised emails, and applying and reconciling late fees.  

Adfin Autopilot changes the game. Credit controllers can use Autopilot to intelligently send reminders from the customer’s own email domain, in their tone of voice and in accordance with their existing templates and chasing process.

This means an Adfin customer could import invoice data automatically using Adfin’s existing Bridge AI solution, send and chase invoices intelligently using Autopilot, and collect and reconcile payment—with no manual work required at all.

Initial Adfin data shows Autopilot can save the typical small to medium-sized business up to 150 hours a month, getting them paid on average 73% faster.

‍Upgrading Adfin’s market-leading collections capabilities  

More ways for the customer to pay means more successful payments, and more money in the bank. Alongside Autopilot, Adfin is launching three fundamental upgrades to its payments platform, bringing total flexibility to the payment experience for client-first businesses:

Bank transfers remain critical to the way many businesses pay. But they require continuous manual work to track and reconcile incoming payments in order to stop invoice chasing. Now, bank transfers can be made directly within Adfin’s payments infrastructure, meaning automatic, instant reconciliation—and no more adding payments manually in accounting software. 

Adfin AutoCollect+ combines card and direct debit options into a single customer journey, meaning less time spent chasing for payment. A business could collect an initial payment on card, with the option to immediately sign a direct debit mandate for future recurring payments. Or if a direct debit mandate hasn’t been signed, a business can automatically switch to offering a card payment. 

And lastly, Adfin is releasing a host of much-requested further features to its core payments offering. Clients can’t always afford to pay for a service in full, up front, so Adfin now supports instalment plans. The collection and reconciliation of these can be fully automated alongside the rest of a business’s payments with Adfin. Adfin’s new Statements feature allows businesses to automate the issuing of statements as well as giving clients a portal where they can view and manage their payments. And direct debit migration allows clients to seamlessly migrate their direct debit mandates to Adfin from their existing provider, without the client needing to take action. Hundreds of clients have already migrated their mandates to Adfin using this feature since its beta launch in September.

Eriona Bajrakurtaj, CEO at Major’s Accounts, said: “Since transitioning [to Adfin], our debtors is now 1/3 of what it was 3 months ago… We are now collecting money we thought we had lost.”

Greg Adams, CEO at Catapault Accounting, said: “As a business that supports small businesses and landlords, I'm always on the lookout for tools that reduce admin, improve cash flow, and make life easier. Adfin ticks all three.”

Tom Pope, Co-founder and CEO at Adfin, commented: “Our mission is to help businesses Just Get Paid, and we are extremely excited to release such a game-changing set of products in pursuit of that goal. In particular, we think Adfin Autopilot is the technology any forward-thinking business needs to adopt to stay ahead: always accurate, always precise, and always on. Customers expect routine tasks to be performed flawlessly, freeing your team for the tasks where the human touch really matters. We’re incredibly excited to be first to market with this and have been delighted by early client feedback”. 

‍

Name: Are late payments holding you back? Here’s how to fix it
Post Body:
Late payments aren’t just an inconvenience—they’re a massive problem for small businesses. A recent survey by the Institute of Certified Bookkeepers (ICB) revealed just how damaging these late invoice payments are:

  • UK small businesses are owed an average of £22,000 in late payments—18% of their invoices.
  • Chasing overdue payments takes up 56.4 million staff hours annually, costing SMEs £6.3 billion.
  • To cover cash flow gaps, businesses spend £684 million each year on additional financing.

And bookkeepers are the ones seeing the impact firsthand—supporting clients who are constantly juggling cash flow because invoices aren’t paid on time. The issue of unpaid invoices in the UK is becoming increasingly problematic for small businesses and self-employed individuals alike.

So, how do you get paid faster when your clients don’t use the same tech—or worse, when they’re the ones struggling with late payments?

‍

Take control when your client’s tech isn’t up to scratch

Firms often bear the burden of overdue invoices, manually chasing clients and reconciling payments across disconnected systems. And it’s costing businesses billions.

Adfin bridges those tech gaps, making it easy for all clients to pay on time—even the ones who ghost your emails. 👻📧

‍

Name: Automated payment chasing vs. collection agencies explained
Post Body:
Unpaid invoices are one of the most persistent headaches for small and mid-sized businesses. According to a recent survey, 56% of small businesses reported being owed money from unpaid invoices, averaging $17,500 per business (Intuit QuickBooks). That's cash trapped in limbo, unable to fund payroll, stock, or growth.

When invoices go unpaid, businesses typically face two paths: automated payment chasing or handing the account to a collection agency. Both aim to recover what you're owed, but they operate at different stages, carry different costs, and leave very different impressions on your customers. Understanding how they compare helps you build a smarter accounts receivable (AR) strategy, one that collects faster without burning bridges.

What is automated chasing and how does it work?

Automated payment chasing is software-driven invoice follow-up that runs from within your business. Instead of manually emailing or calling customers about overdue bills, the platform sends scheduled, personalised reminders before and after each invoice due date. These reminders go out via email, SMS, or even WhatsApp, depending on the tool.

The key distinction is timing. Automated chasing is proactive. It nudges customers when a payment is approaching, not just after it's late. Reminders are typically branded with your company's name and tone, so they feel like a natural extension of your relationship rather than a threatening letter from a stranger.

Platforms like Adfin take this further by integrating directly with accounting software such as Xero and QuickBooks. This means invoice data stays synchronised, reminders reflect accurate balances, and payments are reconciled automatically. The result is a hands-off process that keeps cash flowing while you focus on running your business.

The impact of this kind of automation is measurable. Companies that automate more than half of their AR processes report a 32% decrease in Days Sales Outstanding (DSO), equivalent to a reduction of 19 days (SolveXia). That's nearly three fewer weeks waiting for money you've already earned.

How do collection agencies differ?

Collection agencies operate on an entirely different model. They're third-party firms that step in after an invoice has gone significantly overdue, typically 60, 90, or even 120 days past due. When you hand an account to an agency, they take over communication with your customer and attempt to recover the debt on your behalf.

Most agencies work on a contingency basis, meaning they charge a percentage of whatever they successfully collect. Fees commonly range from 20% to 50% of the recovered amount, depending on the age and size of the debt. Some agencies also charge flat fees or require minimum commitments.

The tone of agency communications tends to be more formal and assertive. While reputable firms follow legal guidelines, the shift from your brand's voice to an agency's can feel jarring to customers. This is why 60% of small business founders say they avoid confronting customers over delinquent bills for fear of damaging the relationship (Old National Bank). For many, handing off to an agency feels like crossing a line they can't undo.

What is the difference between automated chasing and outsourced collection agencies?

While both approaches aim to recover unpaid invoices, they differ across several important dimensions. Here's a clear comparison:

  • Cost structure: Automated chasing tools typically charge a flat subscription or per-transaction fee, making costs predictable. Collection agencies take a percentage of recovered funds, which can significantly eat into the amount you actually receive.

  • Customer relationship impact: Automated reminders come from your business, in your tone, preserving the customer relationship. Agency communications come from a third party and often carry a more confrontational tone.

  • Timing in the AR lifecycle: Automation works across the entire invoice lifecycle, from pre-due-date nudges to post-due follow-ups. Agencies typically only engage once a debt is severely overdue.

  • Control: With automated chasing, you decide the messaging, frequency, and escalation path. With an agency, you hand over control of the customer interaction entirely.

  • Speed of intervention: Automated systems act immediately and consistently. Agencies may take days or weeks to begin outreach after receiving an account.

The data supports the value of early, automated intervention. AR automation has helped finance teams achieve a 33-day reduction in DSO and a 50% reduction in 90-day aged accounts (Tesorio). Fewer invoices reaching the 90-day mark means fewer accounts that ever need an agency in the first place.

When does each approach make the most sense?

Automated payment chasing is the right fit for the vast majority of outstanding invoices. Most late payments aren't malicious. Customers forget, lose the invoice in their inbox, or simply need a gentle prompt. Automation handles these cases efficiently without human effort.

Collection agencies, on the other hand, are best reserved for accounts that have genuinely gone cold. If a customer has ignored multiple reminders over 90 or more days and shows no intention of paying, professional debt recovery may be the only option left. This is particularly true for larger sums where the potential recovery justifies the agency's fee.

The numbers highlight why acting early matters. 47% of small businesses reported a portion of their invoices were overdue by more than 30 days, with nearly 1 in 10 invoices falling into this category on average (Intuit QuickBooks). An automated system catches these invoices at the 30-day mark and applies consistent pressure, reducing the chance they ever age into collection territory.

Can automated chasing and collection agencies work together?

Absolutely, and this is where the smartest AR strategies live. Rather than viewing automated chasing and collection agencies as competing options, think of them as complementary stages in a single workflow.

Automation handles prevention and early intervention. It ensures every invoice receives timely, polite follow-up from day one. When a customer pays after the second or third reminder, the system resolved the issue without any human involvement and without any relationship damage.

For the small percentage of accounts that don't respond to automated outreach, escalation to a collection agency becomes the logical next step. Some platforms even offer built-in escalation paths that connect to vetted collection partners, making the handoff seamless.

This layered approach pays off in measurable ways. Companies using AR automation have seen a 10-15% reduction in bad debt write-offs, and automated invoicing alone leads to a 15% drop in bad debts (Resolve Pay). By catching overdue invoices early, you shrink the pool of accounts that need aggressive recovery.

Additionally, 85% of CFOs at companies that have automated more than half of their AR processes cited a decrease in DSO (NetSuite). The pattern is clear: automation first, agency escalation as a last resort.

Adfin's platform supports this layered approach by automating payment chasing across multiple channels while keeping your accounting data in sync. When escalation is needed, having a clean record of all automated touchpoints gives any collection partner the context they need to act quickly.

FAQs

Will automated payment chasing damage customer relationships?

No. Automated reminders are sent in your brand's voice, with personalised messaging and a polite tone. Customers see them as a routine part of doing business, similar to receiving a receipt or order confirmation. Unlike agency letters, automated chasers don't carry the stigma of formal debt recovery.

How much do collection agencies typically charge?

Most agencies charge between 20% and 50% of the amount they recover, depending on the debt's age and complexity. Older debts carry higher fees. By contrast, automated chasing platforms like Adfin use transparent, per-transaction pricing with no monthly fees, so you keep more of what's collected.

At what point should a business escalate to a collection agency?

A common threshold is 90 days past due. If automated reminders, phone follow-ups, and escalation emails have all failed to produce a response, it's reasonable to consider third-party recovery. Some businesses set the threshold at 120 days, depending on the customer relationship and invoice size.

Can small businesses afford automated payment chasing software?

Yes. Many platforms are designed specifically for small and mid-sized businesses, with pricing models that scale with usage. Adfin, for example, charges only per successful transaction with no monthly minimums, making it accessible even for businesses with a small volume of invoices.

Does automated chasing work for B2B and B2C invoices?

Automated chasing works well for both. B2B invoices often involve longer payment terms and established relationships, making polite reminders especially effective. B2C invoices benefit from multi-channel reminders via email, SMS, and WhatsApp, meeting customers wherever they're most responsive.

What happens to customer data when using a collection agency?

When you assign an account to an agency, you share customer contact details and invoice information with a third party. Reputable agencies follow data protection regulations, but you're still handing over sensitive information. With in-house automated chasing, customer data stays within your existing systems.

How quickly can automated payment chasing show results?

Many businesses see improvements within the first billing cycle. Automated reminders sent before the due date often prompt on-time payments that would otherwise have been late. Over a few months, the cumulative effect on DSO and cash flow becomes significant.

Choosing the right strategy for your business

The most effective AR strategy isn't about choosing between automated payment chasing and collection agencies. It's about using both at the right time. Start with automation to catch the majority of late payments early, preserve customer relationships, and keep costs predictable. Reserve agency escalation for the stubborn minority of accounts that have exhausted every other option.

For small and mid-sized businesses, the priority should be reducing the number of invoices that ever reach the collection stage. Automated platforms handle this at scale, freeing your team to focus on growth rather than chasing payments. The result is healthier cash flow, stronger customer relationships, and fewer write-offs.

Name: Bridging the £65 billion SME credit gap: how small businesses can take control of cash flow
Post Body:
A recent report from Allica Bank, Rebooting SME Finance to Unlock Growth, revealed a worrying figure: there’s now a £65 billion gap in credit available to UK SMEs. It’s a stark reminder that many small and medium-sized businesses are struggling to access the finance they need to invest, grow, and manage day-to-day cash flow.

The findings show a long-term trend that’s left small businesses short of support. According to Allica, overdrafts once made up 30% of SME finance in the 1990s but now account for just 5%, while loan rejection rates have soared to 40%. Even more striking, only one in four SMEs now applies for external finance at all — down from around two-thirds a few decades ago.

As the report notes, “The UK has drifted toward property, not productivity.” Lending has shifted towards real estate, leaving productive business investment underfunded.

But while the funding system clearly needs reform, small businesses don’t have to wait for policy change. There’s another side to the story — one that’s entirely within their control.

Why borrowing isn’t the only answer

The SME credit gap highlights a structural challenge, but the day-to-day cash flow pain often comes from somewhere else: unpaid invoices, weak credit terms, and inconsistent follow-up.

For many businesses, the biggest untapped source of working capital isn’t a new loan — it’s the money they’re already owed.

Research from Sage (May 2025) found that tackling late payments could unlock £112 billion in additional cash flow for UK small businesses — almost double the size of the current SME credit gap (Sage, 2025). That means the potential solution is sitting inside SMBs’ own ledgers.

That’s why better credit control has become a survival skill. By tightening processes and automating payments and reconciliation, SMBs can reduce dependency on lenders and build resilience from within.

How small businesses can take control

Here are practical steps to help bridge your own version of the credit gap.

1. Review your receivables process
Start with visibility. How long do invoices really take to get paid? Which clients regularly miss deadlines? Map your average days outstanding and total overdue value — you’ll often find your biggest “loan” is to your own customers.

2. Set and enforce clear credit terms
Consistent credit policies protect cash flow and relationships. Be explicit about payment deadlines, interest on late payments, and escalation processes. Most late payers respond faster when expectations are clear and consistent.

3. Automate reminders and collections
Manual chasing is slow and inconsistent. Automated reminders, retries, and escalation rules keep things moving without eating into your team’s time. Adfin’s Autopilot AI, for example, automates reminders and fallback payments so invoices don’t slip through the cracks.

4. Improve reconciliation and visibility
It’s easy for payments to go missing or unallocated. Automated reconciliation ensures every payment is matched instantly, giving you accurate, real-time insight into who has and hasn’t paid.

5. Use data to manage risk
Segment customers based on payment history and financial behaviour. Reliable clients can have more flexible terms; new or high-risk clients may need tighter limits. Real-time credit visibility helps you act before a late payment turns into a bad debt.

Smarter partnerships for better cash flow

Technology can’t solve the £65 billion gap alone, but it can make small businesses far less exposed to it. Platforms like Adfin help firms strengthen the fundamentals — predictable cash flow, accurate reconciliation, and faster payments — while partners like Allica focus on expanding access to responsible lending.

Together, this creates a more balanced ecosystem: one where small businesses can borrow with confidence when they need to, but also collect efficiently and predictably when they’re owed money.

That’s how the UK can start to close the gap — not just by increasing credit supply, but by helping businesses take back control of their own liquidity.

The takeaway

The credit gap might be measured in billions, but its impact is felt in everyday business decisions — when to invest, hire, or even pay suppliers. While government and lenders have a role to play, small businesses aren’t powerless.

By improving credit control, embracing automation, and partnering with providers who put cash flow first, SMBs can create their own bridge across the gap.

Because in 2025, the smartest businesses will be the ones that get paid faster.

Name: Building compliance from day one: reflections from a fintech startup
Post Body:
At Adfin, we are in the early stages of building something ambitious, and getting compliance right from the start is a core part of that. Payments is a world with increasing regulatory expectations, heightened financial crime risk, and pressure to operate resiliently and prudently. It is not enough to treat compliance as a checkbox; it has to be part of our culture and the way we do business.

When you are an early-stage fintech, building a compliance function comes with unique challenges. There is no off-the-shelf playbook. There are trade-offs. Doing the right things at the right time can be the difference between the business surviving or not.

Here is how we are approaching the challenge, what we have learned so far, and where we are going next.

1. Compliance isn’t a silo, it is a shared responsibility

One of the early critical things to get right is the mindset around compliance responsibility. With a small team, everyone is expected to pitch in and do things that might traditionally fall outside their remit. At Adfin, you might see the CEO building office chairs and the Founders Associate driving a van across the UK to meet customers. The same applies to understanding the compliance requirements we face.

We have always been thoughtful about hiring, and having experienced people helps. Many of our team have worked in regulated businesses before and understand the risks and challenges that come with that. It means people often ask the right questions at the right time and are empowered to speak up.

Compliance considerations tend to surface naturally in different areas, from product and engineering to marketing. Rather than treating these as blockers, we see them as signals that show where the business is maturing, where decisions with regulatory implications need more thought, and where people might need more help to reach the right decision.

2. Your partners are your first regulators

In the earliest stages of a fintech, your first real compliance test often comes from your partners. Whether it is a banking provider, a card acquirer, or a commercial partner, these organisations assess your controls, governance, and people before they agree to work with you. They take a risk on you before you start on the long journey to become regulated yourself.

This creates a dynamic where you have to build credibility and trust from day one. You cannot simply say “we will fix this once we are bigger.” You have to show you are taking compliance seriously even before you are authorised in your own right.

Credibility comes from more than just having documents in place. It is in your roadmap, your decision-making, and your attitude to risk. Firms that want to last in this space need to treat compliance as a competitive advantage, not just a cost centre.

3. Balancing commercial pressure with compliance priorities

In an early-stage company, resources are always limited. Commercial pressures inevitably influence how you allocate them, and compliance is no exception. There are always more controls you could build, more policies you could write, more ways to try to make things 100 per cent failsafe.

Where you focus matters. At Adfin, we take a risk-based approach based on our business model, identifying where the greatest risks lie. One of our key customer segments is accountants and bookkeepers. Adfin helps them collect payments from their customers so they can minimise chasing and focus on their business. To support this, we build compliance and anti-money laundering safeguards into our product design, ensuring the platform is used responsibly and securely.

The aim is not to eliminate all risk but to mitigate it where we can now, while learning and adapting as we grow.

4. No off-the-shelf playbook

When you are building a compliance function in a startup, there is no perfect playbook. Every fintech has a different model, risk profile, and partner ecosystem. At Adfin we look at what the law says, consider our collective past experience (including both successes and failures), experiment where it's safe to do so and implement controls. This happens fast.

Some of our controls are shaped by regulator guidance, while others require more tailored solutions for our business. One size does not fit all, and copy-pasting policies and processes from other firms does not work when your product and customer base are different.

5. Why I joined: building, experimenting, and scaling smart

I joined Adfin because I enjoy building. When you are going from 0 to 1, you have to be deliberate and smart about what you do, every day. I value the freedom to experiment. For example, I have used large language models to prototype simple internal tools, from policy checklists to risk-scoring logic. In a large institution, these kinds of efficiencies could take months and multiple sign-offs. In a startup, you can try, iterate, and implement quickly.

Of course, innovation has boundaries. Regulators do not, and should not, care how fast you can build if it puts customers or the financial system at risk. At the end of the day, even though we’re smaller than other more mature firms, the same laws apply and we have to get it right.

6. What is next for us

We are still early in our journey, but we are building our compliance culture deliberately. Some of our next priorities include:

  • Strengthening internal governance without slowing down decision-making
  • Being thoughtful about how we scale — it is easy to “know” our customers well now, but how will we achieve the same depth of understanding as we grow
  • Automating wherever it is safe and sensible to do so
  • Engaging proactively with regulators as we expand

Building a sustainable fintech is not just about growth; it is about earning trust. That trust comes from doing the right thing.

Name: Choosing the right invoicing solution
Post Body:
Invoicing shouldn’t be complicated or time consuming

For businesses, invoicing is a step towards getting paid - and therefore it should be fun! However, many e-invoicing software solutions still involve complicated and time-consuming processes to create, send, chase, and manage invoices. In addition, much of the time information is being double keyed between the invoicing and accounting software - leading to yet more manual work. 

As a result, many small businesses still leave their invoicing management to evenings and weekends -  leading to frustration and delaying the opportunity to get paid. 

Sending invoices immediately can improve your cashflow

Cashflow management is critical to the success of small businesses.. How quickly invoices are sent is integral to cash flow and therefore the success or failure of the business. Simply, getting paid earlier makes more cash available to pay bills. 

Having easily accessible invoicing tools online and via mobile app means that you can manage invoices in just a few clicks. The faster a customer receives an invoice, the faster they can pay it, contributing to overall cashflow improvement.

A high quality digital payment experience gets you paid faster 

Over the past decade, online payments have transformed - up to now innovation has primarily been led by the Ecommerce industry. The most successful retailers have invested large sums intooptimizing their payment processing experience. This is because a great payment experience leads to more purchases. 

Drawing a parallel to invoice payments - a high quality, tailored payment experience does not necessarily improve the likelihood of getting an invoice paid, but it does make the payer more likely to pay immediately on receipt. Name: Direct debit vs. card processors: key differences explained
Post Body:
Why your payment method choice matters for recurring billing

If your business relies on recurring billing, the payment method you choose shapes everything from cash flow predictability to customer retention. Two options dominate the landscape: direct debit and card processing. Both handle repeat payments, but they operate on entirely different rails, with distinct cost structures, failure rates, and implications for growth.

Choosing the wrong one can quietly erode revenue. Choosing the right one, or the right combination, can protect your bottom line and reduce administrative headaches. Here's what you need to know to make an informed decision.

What is direct debit and how does it differ from card processing?

Direct debit is a bank-to-bank payment method. Once a customer authorises a mandate, your business can pull funds directly from their bank account on a set schedule. There's no card number involved, no expiry date, and no middleman card network. Almost nine out of ten British adults have at least one direct debit commitment, and direct debit accounts for the payment of 73% of household bills (Wikipedia).

Card processing, by contrast, routes transactions through card networks like Visa or Mastercard. Your business charges a stored card number, and the payment passes through an issuing bank, an acquiring bank, and the card network itself. Each layer adds a small fee.

The core mechanical difference is straightforward. Direct debit pulls from a bank account that rarely changes. Card processing charges against a card number that will eventually expire, get lost, or be replaced.

How do fee structures compare?

Direct debit providers typically charge a flat fee per transaction, often between 10p and 50p in the UK. This makes costs predictable and keeps them low for higher-value payments. Whether you're collecting £50 or £5,000, the fee stays roughly the same.

Card processors charge percentage-based fees, usually between 1.5% and 3% per transaction, sometimes with a small fixed component. For low-value payments, this might be acceptable. But as transaction values increase, these percentage fees add up quickly. A £1,000 invoice processed by card could cost £15 to £30 in fees, while the same payment via direct debit might cost under 50p.

For businesses processing high volumes of recurring payments, this difference compounds significantly over a year. It's one reason many subscription and membership businesses gravitate toward direct debit for their regular collections.

What about payment failure and churn rates?

This is where the gap between the two methods becomes most dramatic. On average, 15% of recurring card payments fail compared to direct debit payments, which have a failure rate of less than 1% (Mono). The primary culprit for card failures? Expiry and replacement.

According to data from Visa, 30% of all cards change every year, and 35% of customers forget to update their details when a card is lost, stolen, or expired (Checkout.com). Expired debit card accounts are responsible for 12% of declined payments for recurring transactions, while card-not-present transactions experience 3x higher failure rates than in-store payments (CoinLaw).

These failures don't just create administrative work. They drive involuntary churn, where customers leave not because they chose to, but because a billing issue interrupted their service. Studies have found that payment failures account for 20-40% of customer churn in subscription businesses (Host Merchant Services). A Forrester study confirmed that involuntary churn accounts for a substantial 34% of the overall churn rate (IR).

The financial impact is staggering. Subscription companies lose on average 10% of their top-line revenue to involuntary churn annually, costing the subscription industry more than $440 billion each year (Butter Payments). Direct debit sidesteps most of this problem because bank accounts don't expire the way cards do.

Which payment method is better for recurring billing?

The answer depends on your billing model. Direct debit excels for predictable, regular collections: monthly subscriptions, membership fees, retainer payments, and fixed recurring invoices. The low failure rates and flat fees make it ideal for businesses that need reliability above all else.

Card processing is better suited for variable amounts, one-off purchases, or situations where customers expect the flexibility of paying by card. E-commerce businesses, for instance, often need card processing as their primary method. It's also the default for international transactions where direct debit schemes may not be available.

Customer experience matters too. Setting up a direct debit mandate requires bank account details and a brief authorisation process. Card payments feel more familiar for many consumers and involve less perceived commitment. For B2B invoicing, however, direct debit often feels more natural and professional.

How do speed and settlement times compare?

Card payments typically settle within one to three business days, giving businesses faster access to funds. Direct debit processing cycles are longer, often taking three to five business days from initiation to settlement in the UK's Bacs system. Faster Payment-enabled direct debit solutions are narrowing this gap, but cards still win on speed.

That said, direct debit offers more predictable cash flow. Because you initiate the collection on a set date, you know exactly when money will arrive. Card payments depend on customers paying on time, which introduces variability. For businesses managing tight cash flow, the predictability of direct debit often outweighs the speed advantage of cards.

How do you choose the right provider in the UK?

Selecting a provider involves weighing several factors against your specific business needs.

  • Integration complexity - Does the provider connect with your existing accounting software? Seamless integration with tools like Xero or QuickBooks saves significant time on reconciliation.

  • Fee transparency - Look for providers with clear, straightforward pricing. Hidden fees for failed payments, chargebacks, or mandate setup can erode the cost advantage of either method.

  • Business model alignment - Match your payment method to your billing pattern. High-volume, fixed-amount recurring billing favours direct debit. Variable or international billing may need card processing.

  • Scalability - Consider whether the provider can handle your growth without dramatically increasing costs or complexity.

Many businesses benefit from a hybrid approach, offering both direct debit and card payments to different customer segments. A platform like Adfin supports multiple payment methods including cards, direct debits, and open banking, letting businesses offer the right option for each scenario without managing separate providers. This flexibility reduces friction for customers while optimising costs and collection rates for the business.

FAQs

Can you use both direct debit and card processing together?

Yes, and many businesses do. A hybrid strategy lets you offer direct debit for regular, predictable billing while keeping card payments available for one-off charges or customers who prefer them. Platforms like Adfin make this straightforward by supporting both methods within a single system, so you don't need to juggle multiple providers.

Is direct debit more secure than card payments?

Both methods have strong protections, but they work differently. In the UK, the Direct Debit Guarantee entitles customers to an immediate refund from their bank if a payment is taken in error. Card payments are protected through chargeback frameworks managed by the card networks. For businesses, direct debit carries less fraud risk because transactions are initiated by the merchant under an agreed mandate rather than relying on card details that could be compromised.

What are the typical costs for small businesses?

UK small businesses can expect direct debit fees of roughly 10p to 50p per transaction, depending on volume. Card processing fees typically range from 1.5% to 2.9% plus a fixed fee of 10p to 30p per transaction. For a business collecting £500 monthly subscriptions from 100 customers, direct debit might cost £20 to £50 per month in fees, while card processing could cost £750 to £1,450.

How long does it take to set up direct debit?

Setting up direct debit mandates with customers typically takes one to three business days for the initial authorisation. Modern providers streamline this with online mandate setup, making the process quick for both the business and its customers. Subsequent collections are automatic.

Do customers prefer direct debit or card payments?

Preferences vary by context. For regular bills and subscriptions, UK customers are very comfortable with direct debit. For ad-hoc or first-time purchases, cards feel more natural. Offering both options removes friction and lets customers choose what suits them best.

What happens when a direct debit payment fails?

Failed direct debits are typically retried after a short period. Common reasons include insufficient funds or a cancelled mandate. Unlike card failures, there's no expiry-related decline, which is why overall failure rates remain well below 1%. Automated chasing tools can notify customers promptly, further reducing the impact of any failures.

Choosing the right fit for your business

There's no universal winner between direct debit and card processing. The right choice depends on your billing frequency, average transaction value, and customer base. Direct debit delivers lower fees and dramatically fewer payment failures for recurring collections. Card processing offers speed, familiarity, and flexibility for variable or international payments.

Rather than defaulting to one method, evaluate both against your specific needs. For many UK businesses handling regular invoices and subscriptions, direct debit will be the more cost-effective and reliable foundation, with card processing as a valuable complement for flexibility.
