Name: Direct debit vs. recurring payments: key differences explained
Post Body:
If you collect regular payments from customers, you've likely weighed up direct debit against recurring card payments. Both automate billing, but they work in fundamentally different ways. The method you choose affects your costs, cash flow predictability, and even how many customers you retain. For small and mid-sized businesses, getting this decision right can mean the difference between steady revenue and constant payment headaches.

This guide breaks down the core differences between direct debit and recurring card payments, compares their real-world performance, and helps you decide which approach fits your business best.

What is the difference between direct debit and recurring card payments?

Direct debit is a bank-to-bank pull payment. Once a customer authorises a mandate, the business (or its payment provider) pulls funds directly from the customer's bank account on agreed dates. The business initiates each collection, and the money moves between banks without a card network in the middle.

Recurring card payments work differently. The customer provides card details, which are stored securely on file. The business then charges that card at regular intervals. Each transaction passes through the card network (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) and the customer's issuing bank, just like any other card purchase.

The distinction matters because each method carries different risk profiles, cost structures, and failure rates. Direct debit relies on a relatively stable bank account number, while recurring card payments depend on a piece of plastic that expires, gets lost, or is replaced by the issuer.

How does each method handle authorisation?

With direct debit, the customer signs a mandate, a one-time authorisation that gives the business ongoing permission to collect payments. That mandate stays active until the customer cancels it. Because it's tied to a bank account rather than a card, there's no expiry date to worry about.

Card-on-file recurring payments require the customer to share their card details once. However, cards expire every few years, and banks frequently issue replacements after fraud or account changes. When a stored card becomes invalid, the next payment attempt fails unless the customer updates their details. This creates a significant source of involuntary churn, which we'll explore next.

How do direct debit providers compare to card processors for recurring nilling?

Choosing between these two methods isn't just about mechanics. The differences in cost, reliability, and administrative burden are substantial.

Cost structures diverge significantly. Card processors typically charge a percentage of each transaction (often 1.5% to 3%), plus a fixed fee. For high-value or frequent transactions, those percentages add up quickly. Direct debit providers usually charge a flat fee per transaction, regardless of the payment amount. This makes direct debit considerably cheaper for businesses processing larger invoices or high volumes of recurring payments.

Failure rates tell an even more compelling story. On average, 15% of recurring card payments fail, compared to direct debit payments which have a failure rate of less than 1% (Mono). A broader study found that credit card payments have an average failure rate of 7.9%, while digital wallets average 11.5%, compared to just 2.9% for bank debit payments. According to research by Forrester, half of the businesses surveyed experienced a payment failure rate of 7% across all payment methods.

These failures don't just delay revenue. They drive customers away. Studies show that 20 to 40% of churn for subscription-based businesses is involuntary, primarily caused by failed payments (FlyCode). And 70% of companies report that failed payments have negatively impacted their customer churn rates in the last year (Trustly).

Which method offers better cash flow predictability?

Direct debit wins here convincingly. Because bank accounts rarely change, payment mandates stay valid for years. This stability translates directly into more predictable revenue. Using direct debit improves payment success rates, reducing failures from around 10% to 2.9%, allowing a typical subscription business to reduce involuntary churn from 1.8% to 0.36% and overall churn from roughly 6% to 4.5%.

Card payments introduce more volatility. Expired cards, issuer-initiated replacements, and spending limits all create unpredictable gaps in collection. According to Forrester, insufficient funds are responsible for 53% of failures of recurring payments (IR), but card-specific issues like expiry and replacement account for a significant additional share that direct debit avoids entirely.

For businesses that rely on predictable monthly income, fewer payment failures mean easier forecasting, healthier cash reserves, and less time spent chasing late payments. Platforms like Adfin help businesses automate this entire process, combining direct debit collection with AI-driven payment chasing to minimise the administrative burden of failed or late payments.

When should a business choose direct debit over recurring card payments?

The right choice depends on your business model, transaction values, and customer base. Here's a practical breakdown:

Direct debit works best for:

  • Subscription and membership businesses collecting fixed monthly amounts

  • B2B invoicing where transaction values are higher

  • Businesses prioritising low failure rates and cash flow stability

  • Companies operating in the UK (via Bacs) or Europe (via SEPA), where direct debit infrastructure is well-established

Recurring card payments work best for:

  • Consumer-facing businesses with smaller, variable transaction amounts

  • International transactions where direct debit schemes aren't available

  • Scenarios where customers expect to pay by card (e.g., SaaS trials converting to paid plans)

Direct debit accounts for 74% of recurring payments in the UK, reflecting how deeply embedded this method is in British business culture. For UK-based small and mid-sized businesses, it's often the default choice for good reason.

Geography matters too. Bacs Direct Debit covers the UK, SEPA handles the eurozone, and ACH serves the United States. If your customers span multiple regions, you may need a provider that supports several schemes, or a hybrid approach that combines methods.

Adfin supports multiple payment methods, including cards, direct debits, open banking, and bank transfers, letting businesses offer the right option for each customer without managing separate systems.

FAQs

Are direct debits safer than recurring card payments?

Both methods offer consumer protections, but they work differently. In the UK, the Direct Debit Guarantee gives customers an immediate, no-questions-asked refund for any payment taken in error. Card payments rely on chargeback processes, which can take weeks to resolve. From a business perspective, direct debit disputes are rarer because the mandate process sets clear expectations upfront.

Can a business use both direct debit and card payments together?

Absolutely. Many businesses adopt a hybrid approach, offering direct debit for regular invoices and card payments for one-off or smaller transactions. This gives customers flexibility while letting you steer higher-value recurring payments toward the more reliable, cost-effective method. Platforms like Adfin make this straightforward by supporting multiple payment methods through a single integration.

What happens if a direct debit or card payment fails?

When a direct debit fails, the provider typically retries the collection after a few days. The most common cause is insufficient funds. Card failures are more varied: expired cards, spending limits, and issuer blocks all play a role. On aggregate, 26% of total churn is involuntary, occurring not because customers want to leave but because of payment issues like card replacement or insufficient funds (Trustly). Automated retry logic and timely customer communication are essential for recovering failed payments regardless of the method used.

How long does it take to set up direct debit?

Setting up a direct debit mandate typically takes two to three business days for the first collection, as the mandate needs to be registered with the customer's bank. Subsequent collections follow a standard timeline. Card payments can process almost instantly, which is one advantage for businesses needing same-day revenue confirmation.

Is direct debit cheaper than card payments for businesses?

In most cases, yes. Direct debit fees are usually a flat rate per transaction, while card processing involves percentage-based fees that scale with the payment amount. For a business collecting a £500 monthly invoice, a 2% card fee costs £10 per transaction, whereas a flat direct debit fee might be 20p to 50p. Over hundreds of transactions, the savings are substantial.

Do customers prefer direct debit or card payments?

Preference varies by context. For regular bills and subscriptions, many UK customers prefer direct debit because it's familiar and low-maintenance. For online purchases and smaller recurring charges, cards feel more natural. Offering both options lets customers choose what suits them, which can improve conversion rates at checkout.

Can I switch From card payments to direct debit mid-contract?

Yes, though it requires setting up a new direct debit mandate with each customer. The transition is straightforward if you communicate the change clearly and explain the benefits, such as fewer payment disruptions. Many businesses phase in direct debit for new customers while gradually migrating existing card-paying clients.

Choosing between direct debit and recurring card payments comes down to your business model, customer expectations, and how much you value cash flow predictability. For most UK businesses collecting regular payments, direct debit offers lower costs, fewer failures, and more stable revenue. Card payments still have their place for consumer-facing, variable, or international transactions. The smartest approach is often to combine both, letting each method do what it does best while giving your customers the flexibility they expect.

This week’s spotlight is a little different…we’re chatting with Emily, Digital Solutions Manager at Knights Lowe. Unlike our usual founder features, Emily’s role is all about driving internal change: researching, implementing, and advising on tech that makes a growing firm more efficient. She’s one of many Adfin users who’ve helped shape our roadmap: sharing feedback, flagging use cases, and influencing how the product evolves. 

Could you give us an overview of Knights Lowe and the kind of clients you serve?
We’re a general practice. We work with everyone  -  from sole traders to large clients that need audits, across all industries. We don’t have a niche as such, but we’re big enough to have dedicated departments and some staff have their specialisms - we have around 85 staff across three offices. The firm has grown through a mix of acquisitions and organic referrals. There are people who’ve worked here for over 25 years (it’s got a really lovely vibe!). Internally, there’s a great atmosphere, lots of social and charity events, and genuine friendships. Fun fact  -  we even have two sets of identical twins who all work in the same office!

Can you tell us about your role as Digital Solutions Manager and what it involves?
It’s a new role in this firm, I’ve been here nearly a year. I was previously an Operations Manager at a smaller firm, and now I've moved to a bigger practice to specialise in the tech side  -  both internally and in client advisory work. I handle app advisory, training, software setup, and take the lead on improving internal systems and processes. Basically, I try to create efficiencies wherever I can.

With so many referrals coming in, what do you think drives clients to recommend you?
I think our client managers are just brilliant. They take the time to really understand their clients allowing them to provide tailored advice to help clients achieve their goals, whether that be growing their business, mitigating tax or considering succession and exit strategies.  Ultimately it’s about a focus on making them happy. That ethos runs through the firm  -  customer service is key. We host client events like golf days and go-karting and run seminars whenever there’s a new budget. We invite clients along, which helps build really strong relationships. I hadn’t experienced that before joining here, and it makes a big difference. We consistently attract more clients, often through referrals so we are always growing (and recruiting)!

When you joined the firm, were there specific challenges you were brought in to solve?
The firm had grown so much, particularly via acquisitions, that it reached a point where they needed someone dedicated to researching and implementing new tech, so my CV came at the right time. I’d been in a similar position in my previous role – watching hours of webinars, engaging with others in digital accountancy forums, and attending events like XeroCon and DAS (Digital Accountancy Show), talking to multiple tech providers. One of my recent projects has been to implement a Direct Debit solution, that’s how I came across Adfin.

What prompted your decision to start using Adfin, and what problem were you looking to address?
We’ve been using Adfin for a few months now, and it’s been a refreshing change – your support is excellent. The better rates were a strong incentive, but what really stood out was the absence of chargeback fees when a mandate collection fails – a real plus compared to other providers as these can quickly add up. We also value the built-in automation: clients receive reminders to sign their mandates, reducing the need for manual follow-up. What sealed it for me was the control Adfin offers over the integration. We can set caps on payment limits, by payment type, helping to manage risk when billing larger fees. The roadmap is also packed with features I know we’ll need – they’re clearly listening to firms like ours!

You’ve been a big part of shaping our roadmap with your suggestions - including the upcoming payment link feature. What are you hoping it will help with once it’s live?
I’ve been working with the team on how I’d like it to work. One of the things our MD wants is the ability to take deposits upfront  -  before an invoice is even raised. Payments on account, basically. It’s great that I’ve been able to give feedback directly and influence how the product is being built. It feels like I’ve got a tech partner who’s custom-building something for our needs  -  though I know it’ll help other firms too!

What’s your approach to adopting new tools - is it usually needs-first or tech-first?
A bit of both! Sometimes I think people don’t realise they need something until they see it. I usually know what I need to achieve  -  I just don’t know how yet, so I research! I’m not usually an early adopter - I usually jump on board with the early majority (when the product is further in its development phase) but Adfin is one of the few products I jumped on early because it solved a very specific need we had.

I’m also not afraid to find software engineers on LinkedIn and ask for new features I need!

How would you describe your overall mindset when it comes to implementing change?

I love change - only at work, though! In my personal life, I like routine and structure - I’ve even always lived in the same village! But at work? I thrive on change. I love making improvements, introducing new tech, and creating efficiencies. It’s so satisfying to help implement something our MD had wanted to do for years but never had the tools or the right person to make it happen.

Joining a larger firm has been a big learning curve - communicating change across multiple teams and offices has been challenging. I’ve definitely made mistakes, but I’m learning a lot and continuing to adapt along the way.

What’s your favourite Adfin feature - and why does it stand out for you?
Definitely the control via Xero branding themes. It’s simple but really powerful.

I also love that Adfin sends three automatic reminders. Now I don’t need to set diary reminders  -  it just handles it.

Is there a common misconception about Adfin that you think more people should be aware of?
Yes. People think GoCardless and Adfin are interchangeable, but they’re not. The integrations are completely different. Adfin is built for accountants  -  you can tell it’s been designed with us in mind. There’s just so much more flexibility and depth to the integration with Xero. It’s a different level of tool altogether.

Are there any upcoming tech trends that you're especially excited to explore or implement?
I’m excited about AI - I’m a huge ChatGPT fan! I think Making Tax Digital for Income Tax is going to be a huge shift. That’s my next big project. I’m creating a whole new business model for it using Socket and Adfin. So I am excited about how tech can make that easier!

What’s one task you really enjoy - and one you’d happily never do again?
I hate filling out forms. Especially by hand, my handwriting is terrible! There’s just something so boring and daunting about it  -  even though I love structure, I’ll often mess up the boxes!

Are there any personal tools, apps, or technologies you're currently loving?
I’ve made my house super smart. I control my heating with the Nest app, I’ve got a smart doorbell, smart lights... I just want an easy life! I don’t want to do things manually if tech can do it better!

I swear by Google Assistant for my shopping list. I’ll just say, “Hey Google, add caster sugar to my shopping list.” Then when I’m at the supermarket - it’s all there. Total game changer. You don’t have to stop cooking to find a pen or worry about leaving the list on the fridge. I love it.

Name: Enhancing collections: multi-channel payment chasing guide
Post Body:
Why single-channel payment chasing falls short

Late payments cost businesses far more than just the unpaid invoice amount. The average annual cost from late payments is $39,406 per company, with 10% of companies suffering over $100,000 in related expenses (The Kaplan Group). Despite these staggering figures, many businesses still rely on a single email reminder and hope for the best.

The problem runs deeper than just lost revenue. 89% of businesses say late customer payments have set back their long-term growth goals (Old National Bank). Yet 60% of small business founders say they avoid confronting customers over delinquent bills for fear of damaging the relationship. This tension between needing to collect and wanting to preserve goodwill is exactly where multi-channel payment chasing comes in.

This guide walks you through a tactical approach to collections that uses compliant, multi-channel escalation sequences. You'll learn how to reduce friction, collect evidence for disputes, and maintain the client relationships your business depends on.

What is multi-channel payment chasing and why does it work?

Multi-channel payment chasing is a coordinated approach to sending payment reminders across multiple communication channels, including email, SMS, WhatsApp, and phone. Rather than repeatedly sending the same email, you meet customers where they're most responsive.

The logic is straightforward. Different people prefer different channels. Some check email religiously. Others respond faster to a text message. By diversifying your outreach, you increase the odds of your reminder being seen and acted upon. Businesses can improve their total collection performance by up to 25% when they coordinate efforts across multiple touchpoints (Resolve Pay).

The channel data reinforces this. SMS messages achieve a 98% open rate, compared to email's average open rate of approximately 20-28% (Notifyre). When your reminder actually gets read, you're already halfway to getting paid.

How does an escalation sequence typically work?

An effective payment chasing sequence follows a tiered structure that gradually increases urgency while keeping the tone professional. Here's a practical framework:

  1. Friendly reminder (1-3 days past due): A polite email with the invoice attached and an embedded payment link. Assume the customer simply forgot.
  2. Second touchpoint (7 days past due): Follow up via SMS or WhatsApp with a brief, conversational nudge. Keep it short and include a direct link to pay.
  3. Formal notice (14 days past due): Send a more structured email referencing payment terms and the outstanding amount. Shift the tone from casual to business-like.
  4. Final warning (30 days past due): A clear communication outlining consequences, such as account suspension, late fees, or referral to collections. This can be delivered via phone call or formal letter.

The key is consistency. Each stage should have a defined timeline, a specific channel, and a clear tone shift. This prevents chasing from feeling random or aggressive to your customers.

How do you stay compliant across channels?

Reaching customers on multiple channels means navigating multiple sets of regulations. Getting this wrong can expose your business to fines and reputational damage. Here are the core compliance considerations:

  • Consent: Under GDPR and similar frameworks, you need explicit consent before contacting customers via SMS or WhatsApp for payment reminders. Build consent collection into your onboarding process.
  • Opt-out mechanisms: Every message, regardless of channel, should include a clear way for the recipient to opt out of future communications on that channel.
  • Frequency limits: Bombarding a customer with daily messages across every channel isn't just ineffective, it can constitute harassment. Define maximum contact frequencies per channel per week.
  • Data protection: Payment amounts and account details shared via SMS or messaging apps should be minimised. Direct customers to a secure payment portal rather than including sensitive details in the message body.

Documenting every touchpoint is essential. Keep records of when each message was sent, through which channel, and what it contained. This audit trail protects you in disputes and demonstrates regulatory compliance.

What evidence should you collect for dispute protection?

When a customer disputes an invoice or claims they never received reminders, your evidence trail becomes your strongest asset. Focus on collecting:

  • Timestamped delivery receipts: Proof that the message was delivered to the recipient's device or inbox, with exact date and time.
  • Read confirmations: Where available (especially on WhatsApp and some email platforms), log when messages were opened.
  • Payment-link click tracking: Record when a customer clicked a payment link, even if they didn't complete the transaction. This demonstrates they were aware of the outstanding balance.
  • Call logs and notes: For phone-based escalations, maintain summaries of conversations with dates and agreed next steps.

This evidence serves a dual purpose. It's both a compliance safeguard, proving you followed proper procedures, and a dispute resolution asset if a customer challenges the debt.

How can automation reduce collections friction?

Manually tracking dozens or hundreds of outstanding invoices across multiple channels is unsustainable. Automation transforms payment chasing from a time-consuming chore into a background process that runs reliably.

Compared to single-channel campaigns, omnichannel outreach generates an ROI almost 5x greater (beehiiv Blog). Automation is what makes true omnichannel execution feasible for small teams.

Here's what effective automation looks like in practice:

  • Scheduled reminders: Pre-configured sequences that trigger automatically based on invoice age. No manual intervention needed until escalation.
  • Payment-link embedding: Every reminder includes a unique, trackable link that takes the customer directly to a payment page.
  • Ledger syncing: When a payment is received, the system automatically updates your accounting software and stops the chasing sequence. No duplicate reminders after payment.

Platforms like Adfin automate payment chasing across email, WhatsApp, and SMS while syncing with accounting tools like Xero and QuickBooks. This integration means your team spends less time on administrative follow-ups and more time on relationship management for high-value accounts.

What role do embedded payment links play?

Every additional step between a reminder and actual payment is a point where customers drop off. Embedded payment links eliminate that friction by letting customers pay directly from the message they received.

75% of consumers prefer to receive appointment and payment reminders via text message (beehiiv Blog). Pair that preference with a one-tap payment link, and you've created the shortest possible path from reminder to resolution.

Beyond one-off payments, offering recurring payment options, such as direct debits or card-on-file arrangements, acts as a preventive collections strategy. When customers authorise automatic payments, late invoices become far less common in the first place. Adfin supports multiple payment methods including cards, direct debits, and open banking, giving customers flexibility while ensuring businesses get paid on time.

FAQs

How many reminders should you send before escalating?

Most businesses find that two to three reminders per escalation tier works well. Send an initial reminder, a follow-up three to five days later, then escalate to the next channel or tone level. The total sequence from friendly reminder to final warning typically spans 30 days, though this varies by industry and invoice size.

Can you chase payments via WhatsApp legally?

Yes, but you need prior consent. Under GDPR and similar regulations, the customer must have opted in to receive business communications via WhatsApp. Include WhatsApp consent in your terms of service or onboarding forms. Always provide an opt-out option and avoid sharing sensitive financial details in the message itself.

What tools help manage multi-channel payment chasing?

Look for platforms that combine automated chasing with payment processing and accounting integration. The best tools let you configure escalation rules, embed payment links, and track engagement across channels from a single dashboard. Adfin, for example, unifies invoice creation, multi-channel chasing, and reconciliation in one platform with transparent per-transaction pricing.

How do you avoid damaging customer relationships during collections?

Tone and timing matter more than the number of reminders. Start with the assumption that the customer forgot, not that they're avoiding payment. Use polite, professional language in early stages. Reserve firmer language for later escalation tiers. Automating the process also removes personal tension, as the reminder feels systematic rather than personal.

What's the most effective channel for payment reminders?

SMS consistently outperforms other channels for response rates. Text message outreach generates 45% higher response rates than email communications in collection scenarios, with SMS achieving a 45% response rate compared to email's 6% (Notifyre). However, the most effective approach combines channels rather than relying on any single one.

Should you charge late payment fees?

Late payment fees can incentivise timely payment, but they should be clearly outlined in your terms before the invoice is issued. Springing unexpected fees on customers damages trust. If you do charge fees, mention them in your escalation sequence so the customer understands the consequences of continued delay.

Building a repeatable collections framework

Effective payment chasing isn't about being aggressive. It's about being systematic. A well-designed multi-channel approach balances persistence with professionalism, giving customers multiple opportunities to pay through their preferred method while building the evidence trail you need for compliance and dispute resolution.

Start by mapping your escalation sequence. Define the channels, timing, and tone for each stage. Then automate as much of the process as possible so your team can focus on the relationships that matter most. The businesses that collect consistently are the ones that treat chasing as a documented, repeatable workflow rather than a reactive scramble.

Name: Feel like you’re overpaying for payment fees? Here's how fees work and why you might be paying to subsidise other businesses
Post Body:
Have you ever wondered why accepting electronic payments is so expensive? Here we’ll break down the components of those payment processing fees and outline how you can reduce them. 

‍

What drives payment fees?

When accepting payments, a business typically pays two types of fees: a 'fixed fee,' which is a set charge per transaction regardless of amount, and a 'percentage fee,' which is calculated as a percentage of the transaction amount. To understand what drives those fees, we’ll first need to cover some key concepts for for payment gateway and processor operations. 

  1. Chargeback: If someone pays using a card or direct debit, they can request a chargeback, which is essentially a request to reverse the transaction. For example, if a customer believes their card was used fraudulently, they can ask their bank to issue a chargeback. Payment networks like Visa, Mastercard, and Bacs have rules that determine if a chargeback request is valid.
     
  2. Fraud: this comes in many forms when accepting payments. Types of fraud can be placed into two buckets: some text
    1. Payer fraud: When someone uses stolen payment credentials or initiates a payment with the intention of later disputing it to try and reverse the transaction.
    2. Business fraud: When a business impersonates another legitimate business to request payments or when it falsely advertises products or services that don’t exist.
  3. Liability: typically either the payer’s bank or the business accepting the payment is liable for the payment reversal in the case of fraud or a chargeback. The rules for when each party is liable are also governed by the payment schemes. 

‍

Where do your payment fees go?

While small businesses pay the entire payment processing fee to their payment gateway or processor,, the provider itself only retains a portion of this fee. This retained portion helps cover operating costs, which vary based on chargebacks, fraud, and liability. Here’s what the breakdown of credit card processing fees looks like:

  1. The payer’s bank fee: for card payments, this is referred to as “interchange” and is between 0.2% - 0.3% of a personal card and 1.0 - 1.9% for a business card. 
  1. The payment scheme fee: paid to the operator of the payment network (e.g. Visa, Mastercard, Bacs) - this is typically a low fixed fee plus a % of transaction value. This normally makes up 0.05% - 0.20% of a payment value. 
  1. Payment provider fees: the portion which is retained by your payment processor. These cover fees and additional margin for: some text
    1. Payment processing - to cover the provider’s technical investments and ongoing costs to process payments
    2. Fraud prevention - for tools used to prevent payer and business fraud 
    3. Chargebacks prevention and dispute management - for the tools to prevent and manage chargebacks, and the administrative overheads 
    4. Credit risk arising from liability when processing payments - in the event a business accepting payment fails and goes into administration, the payment provider has the liability for all chargebacks raised against the business that the business cannot fulfil, creating a credit risk

Here’s the catch - certain industries have a much higher rate of fraud, chargebacks and credit risk. In particular businesses operating in online retail, travel and gambling / trading. Although the underlying costs of serving these businesses are higher, payment processors blend their fee into a single, standard rate offered to all businesses. 

‍

What does this mean for you? 

If you are in a lower risk industry (e.g. accounting and bookkeeping) and use a payment gateway that serves higher risk industries, you are in effect subsidising the fees for those customers. You are paying the same amount for your payments as an online retailer, despite having a lower cost to serve. In general, high risk businesses can be 0.5 - 0.8% more expensive to serve for payment processors. 

‍

How can you avoid this?

At Adfin, we’ve built our business payments platform to help services businesses, including accountants and bookkeepers, get paid faster and at lower cost. By focusing on industries with lower rates of fraud and chargebacks, we can pass our savings directly back to our customers.

We keep things simple. It’s free to create an account, there are no monthly fees, and no minimums. We just charge 1.0% + 20p per successful transaction, which is competitive when compared to Stripe fees or Worldpay charges in the UK.

Interested in learning more about our payment processing system and how it can improve your cash flow management? Visit our Pricing and Transparency Manifesto to see how Adfin can work for your business.

By understanding the various components of merchant fees, businesses can take steps to optimize their payment strategies. Different types of transactions may come with varying costs, so selecting the right payment processor is essential.

Name: From buildings to backend: Patrick’s journey into payments
Post Body:
This week in our Employee Spotlight series, we’re introducing Patrick, one of our brilliant backend engineers here at Adfin. Patrick brings deep expertise in payments and a genuine love for clean architecture, shaped by a journey that began with dreams of designing buildings but quickly pivoted to building elegant systems in code instead. Originally from Malta, Patrick has worked on some of the most complex payment challenges out there (instant bank transfers? nailed it). When he’s not deep in code, you’ll find him globetrotting in search of great food and even better wine, or crushing a strategy game. Let’s get to know him a bit more.

What inspired you to pursue a career in software engineering?

I originally aspired to be an architect, but growing up in Malta, I figured there were only so many buildings our small island needed. My passion for problem-solving led me to software engineering instead. After writing my first program in Turbo Pascal in secondary school, I knew I had found my path. That first moment of building something useful was unforgettable and I’ve been hooked ever since.

Why did you decide to join Adfin?

I chose to join Adfin because I thrive in startup environments that offer full end-to-end ownership and a fast-paced delivery culture. Additionally, having spent most of my career in the payments domain, Adfin's innovative approach to simplifying invoice payments presented an exciting opportunity to view the payments space from a different perspective.

What’s the most interesting or challenging project you’ve worked on so far?

At Freetrade, I served as the payments subject matter expert, with my first project focusing on implementing instant bank transfers. This was interesting to me because I got my first taste of the intricate nuances of banking deposit data, including challenges like truncated names, missing details, and varying behaviours across different banks.

When you’re not coding, what do you enjoy doing in your free time?

I love travelling, especially when good food and wine are involved. I also enjoy playing strategy games, whether that’s on the Xbox or a board game.

What’s your favourite book, movie, or TV show?

I have fond memories of growing up with the excitement for the next Harry Potter book or movie, although the books are better in my opinion - Goblet of Fire is my favourite if I had to pick. I’m curious to see how the new TV series turns out.

‍

Big thanks to Patrick for giving us a peek into his journey - from his Turbo Pascal beginnings to tackling tricky bank transfer data. We’re thrilled to have him bringing his calm precision (and sharp eye for strategy) to the team. Keep an eye out for our next spotlight as we share more stories from the people building Adfin behind the scenes.

Name: From fashion to finance: how Beth is building a modern practice
Post Body:
Adfin was the easiest thing I set up in my entire practice: cost-effective, simple, and it just works.

In the spotlight this week is Beth, who swapped a decade in fashion buying at Marks & Spencer for life as an accountant. Bringing a sharp commercial focus and a love of speed, she’s built a modern, tech-driven practice with a personal touch - starting with direct debits from day one and making Adfin one of her easiest (and most impactful) tools.

Can you tell us a bit about yourself and how you got into accounting?

In my previous life, I was a clothing buyer living in London. I did that for about 8 to 10 years, but after going through a few recessions and cutbacks, the role became increasingly focused on budgets and numbers. I actually found myself enjoying that part more and more.

Eventually, I started studying AAT on the side while still working, and then made the switch - it’s been the best decision I ever made.

I’m really passionate about combining all my experience into my own practice - not to do something wildly new, but to drive something better. I saw the extremes: very tech-driven firms and very old-school ones, and I wanted to create something that felt more balanced. I’m big on leveraging tech to give clients more access to me - someone to talk to.

Was there anything from your fashion career that helps you now as an accountant?

Absolutely - speed! In retail, especially a FTSE 100 company, if it wasn’t done yesterday, that wasn’t fast enough. That mindset of being fast and commercially focused really shapes how I work now. I also bring a lot of commercial awareness - knowing when a plan needs sticking to or pivoting - and I think that adds something different to my client work.

Are there particular types of clients or industries you’re focusing on?

For me, the niche is the person. Some people just want to hand over papers and have the work done - and that’s totally fine, but that’s not me.

I want to work with people who are open to change, who want to make their lives easier, and who are happy to collaborate. It’s not about growth for the sake of growth - it’s about figuring out what they want, and helping them get there.

I do have a passion for supporting startups. I’m even working with a local CIS to offer a free mentoring programme in conjunction with a local start up grant for 18-30 start ups. 

Let’s talk more about that tech roadmap - how did you choose what to start with?

There’s so much tech to choose from - client portals, management software, receipt capture tools… It’s endless. I took everything I’d learned so far and chose a stack I felt good about, while keeping an eye on what’s coming up and listening to what other business owners are saying.

One big piece of advice I heard from almost everyone was to set up with direct debits from day one. It takes so much stress off your plate. And it sets you up to scale - you don’t want to be sorting that out later when you’re already swamped.

That’s also how I came across Adfin - at Engager Day. I already planned to use Engager, and when I saw Adfin’s integration was announced, it just made sense. The presentation helped dispel some common myths I had about payments, and honestly, it was the easiest thing I’ve set up so far. Cost-effective, simple, and just works.

Are there any tech trends you’re especially excited about?

There’s really only one answer: AI.

Right now, I’m particularly interested in AI being built into receipt capture tools - not just machine learning, but actual AI. It’s an area that’s still really time-consuming and costly, and clients often don’t fully see the value. So if AI can improve that, I’m all in.

I’ve also automated quite a bit using Client Engager, which has really helped with admin and scaling.

What’s one task you’d happily never do again - and one you love doing?

I’ll start with what I love: cleaning my house. I know it sounds sad, but it’s true! A full clean on a Friday evening really helps me unwind. There’s just something so satisfying about it.

As for what I’d never do again? Talk to HMRC. The setup, the inefficiencies - it’s just painful. Coming from a commercial background, it’s hard to believe they operate the way they do.

Name: From football boots to bookkeeping: Paul’s journey to 200+ clients
Post Body:
"I moved over 200 clients to Adfin and it was seamless. 89% signed their new direct debit mandate within 3 days."

In the spotlight this week is Paul, who swapped life as a professional footballer for one in cloud accounting. He shares how CASS grew from helping friends onto Xero to supporting 200+ clients, why hands-on support beats ticket numbers, and how Adfin became a game-changer for getting paid.

Can you tell me about Cass and how it got started?
I founded Cloud Accounting Support Services (or CASS) eight years ago. We started as a response to Making Tax Digital for VAT. Initially, it was all about moving people into the cloud, primarily using Xero, but also QuickBooks and FreeAgent. Back then, Sage was charging £900 just for a software upgrade (!), so we started helping people move off that.

It began with moving a few friends into Xero. They introduced me to their accountant, and we ended up transitioning all of their clients into cloud accounting. When we trained people on raising sales invoices and capturing purchase invoices, the response was, "We don’t want to do this…do you know someone who can?" I didn’t want to go back into traditional accounting, but I saw an opportunity to help automate it. That’s when I took on an apprentice and started offering bookkeeping as a service.

That evolved into questions like, “How do we get paid?” So we implemented monthly billing via direct debit through GoCardless. We liked the Xero integration, but their model changed and they started charging for things like automatic retries. We also experienced integration issues because we were early adopters. The service became unreliable.

How did you discover Adfin?
I sent a couple of the team to Engager Labs in Liverpool who met the Adfin team. They came back and told me, “Paul, it does direct debit, on-demand payments, and still integrates with Xero. You need to explore this”. I had a Zoom call with Adfin but didn’t feel ready to make the switch, as we have over 200 clients on direct debit, and I didn’t want payment disruptions.

Eventually, I just bit the bullet. I wrote to clients explaining the switch, shared a link to set up their new mandate, and we went from there. Now, about 90% of our clients are with Adfin. The interface is smoother, everything is in one place, and support is excellent. It’s probably one of the best operational decisions we’ve made.

Have you seen resistance when asking clients to switch platforms?
We didn’t enforce it. We explained the benefits and gave them the choice. Currently, 207 clients pay us regularly, with around 170 using direct debit via Adfin. The rest will move over during their next review cycle. Eventually, we’ll turn off GoCardless and Stripe entirely.

Do you focus on specific industries at CASS?
We’re strong in e-commerce and domiciliary care, mostly because of our payroll expertise and third-party tool knowledge. But we’re more focused on client size rather than industry. Most of our clients are between £80,000 and £2 million in turnover. That’s our sweet spot: businesses on a growth journey that need regular bookkeeping and support.

We don’t take on year-end-only clients. We only do annual year end compliance if we’re involved in day-to-day operations. It gives us complete visibility and makes the year-end process smoother, more efficient and gives us more confidence when we do year end tax planning. If someone calls just for a self-assessment or accounts, we decline. That’s our model.

So you operate more like a consulting firm than a traditional accountancy?
Exactly. Our strapline is “Giving you more than the numbers.” It’s about providing tech stacks that remove unnecessary human input and offering strategic insights. We aim to be a financial conscience - an extension of our clients business who then have confidence and trust to consult with us before making key decisions. That’s one way where we we provide real value.

Who would be your dream client?
So, from a “love to work with” perspective, we’ve tendered for, but would really love to work with, a company called Aconveyancing. They’re just over the road from us. We've had some tentative conversations, but if we could win that, we know we could completely change their workflows and streamline a lot of their manual transactions. That’s my dream client. Hopefully, over the next few weeks, we might be able to secure them.

More broadly, the ideal client for us is a business owner, especially those who want more from an accountant than just compliance. We’re looking for small business owners who want a full-house finance team: from digital accounting technicians who handle data entry, through to monthly management accounts, quarterly reviews, and then advisory services. That includes support around compliance challenges that we all face.

Do you have an example of where this kind of approach made a difference?
Yes - just recently, a client we do bookkeeping for had been chasing their accountant for support for three weeks. In frustration, they rang us and asked for our help. We had a quick chat, gave them some advice, and they walked away extremely happy. That advice took us 10 minutes.

What sets your approach to client support apart from bigger firms?
I think people value quick, available support. We try to make our service really fast and really valuable. Our existing clients all have access to their own member of our team, with their working hours and we’ll always jump in and help. WE deal with 90% of queries via a 2-5 minute phone call.

There’s a human behind everything we do. Sure, we all have chatbots and AI tools, but sometimes you just want a real person who can jump in and help right away. None of that “we’ll reply in 24 hours” or “you’re now ticket number X.” That’s another benefit of working with a smaller, more agile team like ours versus a huge conglomerate.

What’s one fun fact about your journey?
I’m a former professional footballer. I played for Exeter City under Alan Ball. After football, I needed a job, and fell into accounting thanks to a neighbour who helped me get my first job as a purchase ledger clerk. I worked my way through the structure there. That led me to work with companies like Rolls-Royce and Birmingham City Council.

Do you still play or coach football?
I used to coach for years, especially when my sons were playing. My eldest was a pro at Derby and is now their full-time goalkeeping coach. When they stopped needing me as a coach, I shifted to hiking in the Lake District, which I now do every other weekend.

How do you stay ahead with tech?
I spend half a day each week exploring the New Zealand Xero app store. I’ve noticed that most apps on there eventually make their way to the UK. It helps us anticipate what's coming.

Which tech tool has had the biggest impact?
Invoicing and payment tools - especially features like “pay now” links, direct debit, and automated payments. They’ve transformed our (and our clients) cash flow and made things easier for both us and our clients.

How do you use AI in your business?
We use AI for creating documentation, analysing numbers, and streamlining tasks. It helps us save time and deliver deeper more meaningful insights. But we still use a human approach for providing feedback to our clients. AI can’t sit down with a business owner and understand their goals or challenges the way a person can.

What’s your perspective on AI in accounting?
It’s an assistant, not a replacement. AI helps automate repetitive tasks, allowing us to focus on providing strategic advice. Tools like ChatGPT are great, but only in the hands of someone who knows what to ask and how to interpret and use the output.

What’s your go-to drink while working?
Tea - English Breakfast, milk, no sugar.

And when you're not working?
Pepsi Max with lime, no ice. I don’t drink alcohol, so it’s my go-to.

If you could automate anything in your life, what would it be?
Charging my electric car. I keep forgetting to plug it in when I get to work.

Any final thoughts?
Don’t be afraid of change - whether that’s a new accountant or piece of tech or a payment provider. Change can be seamless if done right. We’ve had clients cancel a direct debit from Adfin out of confusion, but once they understood it, they reactivated it immediately. If you do it for the right reasons, it’s a win.

Name: From problem to product: inside Adfin's AI development framework
Post Body:
With AI becoming increasingly popular in recent years, many are wondering whether it is over-hyped and over-used. While time and the market will eventually sort the hype from the lasting value, we will continue to pragmatically build AI products that solve real world problems that would otherwise be unapproachable. To aid the reading of this text, along with our AI development framework, I will also present a concrete example of how it was applied in practice to build an AI-based invoice scanner. This is the first blog post in our AI blog series where we’ll also cover topics such as Data Mining, Data Engineering and Process Optimisation.

What are we solving?

Whenever we consider using AI in a solution, we start by clearly defining the core problem that we are solving and its technical restrictions. As it is the case for any well-posed problem, we must define the input and the output - here the input is an invoice as a file (pdf or image), and the output is a domain specific key-value mapping (e.g. customer email, biller bank details). Multiple functions may satisfy this requirement, and we will evaluate and rank them using business-specific metrics: speed, cost and accuracy.

When should we use AI?

As stated above, we should use AI whenever we want to solve an unapproachable problem. Although this sounds like common sense, there are plenty of cases of LLMs being used instead of a regular expression, and vision models replacing basic image processing snippets. While AI solutions can be reliable, a 99% accuracy leaves room for surprises - deterministic, static solutions are often more reliable and maintainable if they meet the requirements. Scanning invoices is hard - before the current generation of AI models, entire start-ups were founded just to solve this single problem; classifying this invoice ingestion problem as too difficult for a purely engineering solution.

What AI model should we use?

At the moment there are a significant number of AI model providers (including open source models), each offering multiple models with different trade-offs in speed, cost and accuracy. Selecting a single model to use in a product is not trivial. Of course, public benchmarks and ELO tables may guide our decision, but the no free lunch theorem tells us that doing so may trick us into using a sub-optimal solution for our particular problem. Our solution to this model selection meta-problem is to develop problem-specific automatic evaluation benchmarking tools. These allow us to empirically measure speed, cost and accuracy of each model for our specific use case.

The choice of a single model is still not straightforward - the output of multi-objective optimisation algorithms is a front of non-dominated solutions, whereas we would require a clear ranking of the solutions. In such cases, the user preference decides the final solution rankings. For the invoice scanner, the business acceptance criteria defined the user preference rules: the ingestion cost per invoice must be below X cents, the ingestion time must be below Y seconds, rank the remaining models by accuracy.

Build around the AI core

Similarly to the famous expression of Mathematics authors “the proof is trivial and it is left as an exercise to the reader”, an AI Engineer might state that the AI core is validated and the rest of the software product is left to the Software Engineering team. Given the integration complexities usually involved, both statements can only be jocular phrases. To be clear, at Adfin, an AI Engineer’s role does not end with the proof of concept; it extends to developing products from the initial idea all the way to our clients.

AI integration comes with unique challenges beyond standard software development concerns. Let’s discuss them one by one:

  1. Model availability: Outages from AI providers are out of our hands - but our reaction is not. We build AI products that support multiple providers, making it easy to create fallback mechanisms that span across different providers.
  2. Surprising responses: the entire point of using an AI component is to solve difficult problems, translating into highly variable inputs that may lead to unexpected responses. A quite well known example is that of making slight changes to traffic signs in order to trick the vision model of self driving cars. In the absence of ground truth, we log all responses and improve iteratively.
  3. Privacy concerns: financial data is particularly sensible and it must be handled with great care. When building AI products, Adfin only considers model providers that comply with strict privacy and data governance standards.
  4. Scalability: all LLM providers impose maximum concurrency limits, generating scalability bottlenecks. Our solution is an extension of the fallback mechanism: whenever we approach the concurrency limit of one provider, consider routing the following requests to another one - again, in the order of our preference.
  5. User experience: AI takes time. While the model runs, the user interface should reflect that (e.g., show a spinning “in progress” icon or a progress bar). If a response takes too long, we notify users via email to keep them in the loop even after the session ends.

AI can be transformative when applied thoughtfully to hard problems. At Adfin, we view AI as part of a broader product - where business needs, user experience and system reliability are all part of the design. Our invoice scanner demonstrates the impact of this approach: compared to our earlier version built with OCR and text-only models, the new scanner - developed using our AI framework - processes invoices 3x faster, at 1/20th of the cost, and has a reduced error rate from 20% to just 1%.

Name: Growing in Guernsey: how Tim built TCS and beyond
Post Body:
Direct debits have completely changed how we run the business. We get paid on time, every time — and Adfin makes that easy.

In the spotlight this week is Tim, founder of TCS and newly launched 65. What started as a teenage accident in bookkeeping turned into a thriving Guernsey-based practice with plans that reach far beyond the island. Tim shares how a failed startup led to new beginnings, why he refuses to niche down, and how Adfin’s direct debit feature has transformed the way his firm gets paid — making growth in Guernsey smoother than ever.

‍How did you get into bookkeeping and how did TCS start?

I got into bookkeeping by mistake when I was about 16 or 17. I was offered a job at a company one of my friends worked at, and the role was accounts assistant—which was really bookkeeping. I worked in accounts departments at various levels throughout my career, often alongside other jobs. After moving to Guernsey, the startup I worked for failed. Through contacts I made there, I got a six-month system migration contract and a few bookkeeping clients. I’d thought about starting a firm many times, but always chose stability instead of risk. Anyway, that’s how TCS started.

Do you serve particular industries, and do you work only in Guernsey or further afield?

Hospitality and retail make up about 55% of our Guernsey client base. I’ve worked to diversify—people say you have to niche, but you don’t. Our niche is broader: B2C. We have a few B2B clients, but most serve consumers directly. Recently, we’ve added trades like gardeners, plumbers, and a beauty salon. Most clients are in Guernsey, but we have a few in the UK. In September, we’re launching a subsidiary called 65, which will exclusively serve hospitality and retail in the UK.

How does Adfin fit into the launch of 65?

We’ve just launched 65 on September 30th. It’s a UK bookkeeping practice run by TCS, exclusively for hospitality and retail, providing the same high level of service. We’ll use Adfin exclusively, and clients who don’t sign up for direct debit won’t be accepted.

What do people often get wrong about business in Guernsey?

From outside, people assume everyone is wealthy because it’s a tax haven, but that’s not true. We pay plenty of taxes—it’s only corporation tax that’s 0%. Costs of living and wages are high. From within Guernsey, many business owners undervalue good bookkeeping. They spend money they should have saved for tax liabilities, or they copy UK business models without considering Guernsey’s demographics. For example, food delivery apps struggle here because the population is spread out, unlike clustered UK towns.

Before Adfin, how did you get paid and what drew you to use it?

In Guernsey, we had no recurring payment or direct debit options. GoCardless used to support Guernsey but stopped onboarding new clients just as I was starting. So, we relied on standing orders or invoicing at the start of the month and then chasing payments. That sometimes led to bad debt when clients failed. Startups fail often, and sometimes it was just bad luck. Our process really came down to “please pay us.”

What’s your favorite Adfin feature?

Direct debits, 100%. Most clients are on direct debit now. For bad payers, I’ve been firm: either sign up for direct debit or we stop supporting you. It’s important we get paid. If a client is struggling, I now insist they pay us first because we’re doing extra work to keep them afloat. Adfin makes that easy.

Do you have a proud or defining moment with TCS?

I wouldn’t say a single “I’ve made it” moment, but becoming more involved with the ICB over the last three years has been rewarding. We’ve spoken at events, been invited to summits, and become known in that community. Five years ago, I wouldn’t have expected to be asked for interviews and podcasts. It makes me proud—it shows we know what we’re talking about.

What’s one task you love doing and one you’d happily never do again?

I love reconciling messy accounts manually—finding differences, fixing issues, and getting it to zero. It’s geeky but very satisfying. The task I hate most is hoovering. I despise it. Other cleaning is fine, but not hoovering. I even bought a robot hoover for home. The only exception is Henry the Hoover—that’s just about acceptable.

Name: How Adfin beats other payment solutions on cost and value
Post Body:
Adfin's headline prices are attractive, but we often get asked how this compares in real-world examples. In this blog, we'll outline how Adfin compares to a mix of typical alternative providers (GoCardless, Stripe, and Chaser).

Using real-world assumptions for both small and large businesses, the results are clear: Adfin delivers significant savings—while including features others charge extra for.

‍The problem with piecemeal solutions

Many businesses today rely on a patchwork of providers:

  • A direct debit provider like GoCardless for Direct Debit transactions
  • A PSP like Stripe for card payments
  • A tool like Chaser for payment chasing and collections

This setup looks manageable on the surface, but costs add up quickly. Each provider charges their own percentage fees, transaction costs, and add-ons like branding or retries. Chaser alone can add £135 to £675 per month just for automated email chasing.

By contrast, Adfin bundles everything into one transparent, low-cost package—covering Direct Debit, Open Banking, card payments, branding, and fully-featured, unlimited chasing.

Case studies

Setup

To make this comparison realistic, we modelled two types of businesses:

  • Small business: 100 transactions per month, £50 average transaction value (£60k annual turnover)
  • Mid-size business: 1,000 transactions per month, £100 average transaction value (£1.2M annual turnover)

... across 2 scenarios:

  • The "cheapest possible" setup (using the minimum of features in the case of other providers)
  • The "typical" setup (using a more typical range of features)

We assumed the following payment split:

  • 65% Direct Debit
  • 10% Open Banking
  • 25% card payments

These volumes reflect common mixes seen across UK SMEs.

Case study 1: The “cheapest possible” scenario

In this setup, businesses don’t require advanced features or branding. The question is simple: what’s the lowest possible monthly cost?

Small business (100 x £50 average transaction value)
  • Adfin: £70/month
    • Adfin fee of 1% + 20p (1% * 100 transactions *  £50, plus 100 * £0.20)
  • GoCardless + Stripe (no chasing, no branding): £78.75/month
    • Gocardless fee of 1% + 20p = £55.00
    • Stripe fee of 1.5% + 20p = £23.75

Even in this barebones setup, Adfin comes out cheaper.

Mid-sized business (1,000 x £100 average transaction value)
  • Adfin: £1,200/month
    • Adfin fee of 1% + 20p (1% * 1000 transactions * £100 plus 1000 * £0.20)
  • GoCardless + Stripe (no chasing, no branding): £1,325/month
    • Gocardless fee of 1% + 20p = £950
    • Stripe fee of 1.5% + 20p = £425

Again, Adfin is lower cost.

Case study 2: Typical usage, with branding and features

Typically, businesses need more than the most basic package offered by these providers. In this scenario, we have taken Gocardless's middle pricing tier to ensure a comparison to Adfin. In this scenario, the business is using custom chasing, name-on-statement, and custom payment pages.

Small business (100 x £50)
  • Adfin: £106/month (as above, but with the £36/month Adfin Custom add on)
  • GoCardless Advanced (1.25% + 20p) + Stripe (1.5% + 0.4% + 20p) + Chaser (£135 / month): GoCardless £65.13/month, plus £200 a month for custom branding; £28.75 for Stripe; £135 for the most basic Chaser package

That’s a 4x difference. Adfin delivers the same (or better) features for a fraction of the price.

Large business (1,000 x £100)
  • Adfin: £1,236/month (as above, but with the £36/month Adfin Custom add on)
  • GoCardless Advanced (1.25% + 20p) + Stripe (1.5% + 0.4% + 20p) + Chaser (£675 / month): GoCardless £1,125.50 + £200 branding; £525 for Stripe; £675 for the Chaser package with sufficient users and support equivalent to Adfin.

Here too, Adfin saves over 50% per month—while still including chasing and branding.

We see this in the real world

We know the examples above are realistic, because our customers tell us how much they save with Adfin. If you haven't seen it already, check out the Helpbox case study: Helpbox saved 58% on their payment fees by moving to Adfin and have been a happy customer ever since.

Why Adfin wins

  1. Lower fees across the board
    We have modelled the above on standard transactions for all providers to keep things fair (both Adfin and Stripe charge more for non-standard cards for example, with roughly comparable fees). For the majority of transactions, Adfin charges just a combined fee of 1% + 20p per collection , whether it’s Direct Debit, Open Banking, or cards. Competitors charge higher percentages, especially for cards (Stripe starting at 1.5%).
  2. Chasing included (worth £135-675/month)
    Competitors like Chaser charge extra for automated payment reminders. Adfin bakes this in for free, and you get the benefits of an integrated product.
  3. Branding without the premium
    GoCardless Advanced  and Stripe both add branding costs—Adfin includes them in its pricing.
  4. One provider, one invoice
    Managing three or more vendors not only costs more but also adds operational complexity. With Adfin, you have one provider, one support team, and one predictable cost.

The bottom line

For businesses that want to save money without cutting features, Adfin is the clear choice. Whether you’re a small business processing £60k per year or a large enterprise handling millions, the savings stack up month after month.

In short: Adfin doesn’t just save businesses money—it eliminates complexity, improves cashflow, and gives you peace of mind.

Name: How Adfin delivers quality products faster than the speed of light
Post Body:
The best-performing companies I’ve interacted with excel at learning, adjusting, and executing swiftly. In our ever-changing world, customers’ problems and expectations evolve rapidly, and the ability to launch or improve products quickly is key. But speed alone isn’t enough — high quality, reliability, security, availability, and user experience are all essential for products to be trusted and loved by customers.

I’ve had the privilege of working at several successful companies, thinking I had seen the fastest product delivery possible. I’ve discussed product delivery techniques with friends and peers, presented at conferences and industry events. I believed it was impossible to move any faster.

That belief changed a few months ago when I experienced something entirely new. Imagine you're at an amusement park, boarding a seemingly endless and thrilling roller coaster. As the ride starts, your face distorts with the force, and before you can even scream, you’re at the finish line. This intense mix of emotions and adrenaline makes you wonder if it was all a dream and if you’re eager to ride again. That’s how I felt about the speed our team at Adfin achieved recently.

For a concrete example: On June 10th, we released our first beta version to our customers. Just four weeks later, we developed and released three new large products: Pay by Card (Apple Pay, Google Pay, card on file), full 2-way accounting integration with Xero that always reconciles, and our core customizable workflows. This was accomplished with a small team of four engineers (one of whom had joined only a few weeks prior), a designer, and two persons who spent a part of their time as product managers.

Here are the five main ingredients that made this possible:

  1. Strong Company Culture
    While the term "company culture" is often overused, in my experience, it truly is the foundation of a company’s success or failure. At Adfin, we live and breathe our ATHOS (acronym of our values) principles in everything we do. Stay tuned; I’ll delve deeper into this in a future blog post.
  2. Working with the Best People
    My previous role involved leading a large engineering organization with 35 teams across multiple countries. At Adfin, we took a different approach: building a small, elite team capable of moving mountains. You can’t imagine what high-potential, ambitious people can achieve when given the best tools and end-to-end ownership—from infrastructure to backend, frontend, testing, delivery, and customer satisfaction. 
  3. Focused, Well-Bounded Work
    We operate in 4-week cycles plus a delivery/wrap-up week. Each team member owns a project and enjoys focused work time to ensure fast and high-quality delivery. Unlike many teams that waste time estimating work, we use an investment-driven approach. For each project, we ask, “How much do we want to invest in this project?” If we can’t deliver a good product in half a cycle or a full cycle, we don’t start it. This method ensures full commitment from the team to maximize the return on investment.
  4. Fully Cross-Functional Teams
    Our engineers collaborate closely with our designer, and the product manager is involved daily in the work. We also engage customers and prospects in our projects, working with them to understand their problems and validate our ideas. This involves sharing designs, conducting demos, and onboarding beta users for testing. This gives us the ability to build the right product, avoid blockers, and quickly answer questions or concerns.
  5. Quality First Mindset
    Giving end-to-end ownership means our team takes quality as a top priority. From day one, they found healthy ways to automate tests for our product. We rely on a suite of unit, integration, and end-to-end tests (API and User Interface) to guarantee our product works as expected. In just a few months, the team delivered impressive products and capabilities, all validated by 1,049 automated tests, with automated scenarios running non-stop in every environment, including production.

These key ingredients make our team at Adfin - and our customers - feel like they’re teleporting on this journey. Simple practices, executed well by an A-class team, have truly moved the needle!

If you’re curious to learn more, follow our Adfin LinkedIn page. We’ll continue sharing various techniques we use to provide super-fast and high-quality product engineering.

Name: How Adfin puts customers first: our approach to support and operations
Post Body:
If you’re one of our customers, chances are we’ve already met! Whether it was during your onboarding call or through one of our many support channels – email, WhatsApp, Google Meet, or live chat – it’s usually me, Chris from Adfin, on the other end. I love it! Getting to chat with so many customers every day keeps me tuned in to what you’re thinking and feeling.

After six months of helping shape our support processes and making improvements along the way, I thought it was time to give you a quick behind-the-scenes look at how we make sure your customer experience is best in class. It’s what drives us every day – how do we build a product that you truly love? And just as important, how do we support you every step of the way?

Building customer connection and trust

We’ve all been there – dealing with companies that feel faceless and unresponsive, this is especially frustrating especially when it comes to something as critical as accounts receivable. At Adfin, we know how important it is for our customers to feel connected and informed, especially if something goes wrong. Things don’t always go to plan – but what matters is how quickly and transparently we put things right!

Our customer support philosophy is simple: stay proactive, stay human, and stay responsive. Whether it’s a minor issue or something more significant, our team makes sure that you’re always in the loop.

The modern tech stack: Intercom, Linear, and Incident.io

One of the best things about starting a company from scratch is the chance to build a modern tech stack that keeps day-to-day operations seamless. At Adfin, we’ve embraced a tech-forward mindset, using cutting-edge tools to make support and operations as smooth as possible. Our core tools? Intercom, Linear, and Incident.io.

Intercom helps us manage customer interactions effortlessly. From chat support to product updates, it keeps us connected and ensures you’re never left in the dark.

Linear is all about keeping our product roadmap transparent and accountable. We’re passionate about feedback and aim to build products our customers genuinely love. Linear tracks feature requests, bug reports, and development progress, helping us make sure that when a bug is reported, it doesn’t show up again. One of the coolest aspects is how Linear links feature requests directly to our engineering efforts – as soon as a new feature goes live, we can instantly notify the customers who asked for it.

Incident.io is our go-to for handling support escalations and urgent issues. Every week, we pair a customer support on-caller with an engineering “Guardian” to tackle tickets swiftly. We manage this collaboration through Incident.io, where any team member can raise an incident, set its priority, and pull in the right people to a dedicated Slack channel – our version of a “war room” for quick and effective resolutions. This hands-on, team-driven approach is our secret sauce for staying responsive and efficient.

By combining these powerful tools, we make sure that our support and operations are agile, transparent, and always customer-focused.

Experimenting with AI agents: meet Fin!

While staying human is a core pillar of our support philosophy, that doesn’t mean we haven’t dabbled with AI. Our team may be mighty, but it’s relatively small, and as demand for Adfin grows, we’re always looking for ways to make support more efficient – especially after hours. That’s where Fin, our AI helper, comes in!

Letting Fin loose was both exciting and a little nerve-wracking. Sometimes Fin nails it, delivering accurate and helpful answers – about 60% of the time. Around 25% of responses are close but need a little tweaking, and the remaining 15%... well, they miss the mark entirely. We’re constantly refining how we use AI, and while it’s a learning process, it’s exciting to see how far we’ve come!

If you’ve ever been on the receiving end of one of Fin’s more creative responses – sorry about that! We believe the best way to learn is by doing, and that applies to Fin too. Rest assured, I’m always monitoring responses, ready to jump in if Fin goes off track.

When you open up our live chat and select the option “I have a question,” we let Fin take the first shot at answering. If you’re not satisfied, just click “Talk to a person,” and you’ll be straight through to human support. No frustrating AI barriers.

Adfin is still young, and so is Fin. We’re committed to making them smarter and more reliable as we grow – thanks for being part of the journey!

Staying agile with fast-paced development

Adfin’s platform is constantly evolving, thanks to our world-class engineers. It’s a great problem to have, but the speed at which we ship new features and upgrades means Fin’s knowledge base is always playing catch-up. Sometimes, when Fin’s answers are a bit off, it’s not entirely fair to blame them – if you’d asked the same question a week earlier, the response would probably have been spot on!

We’re always working to keep both Fin and our support team up to date. We’re also looking into smarter ways to integrate updates into our support workflows, ensuring that both AI and human responses stay accurate. It’s a challenge, but one that keeps us on our toes and motivated to keep improving – watch this space.

Why the customer always wins

At Adfin, customer support isn’t just another department – it’s a mindset. Building great relationships with our customers is just as important to us as building great products. Whether it’s through genuine human support, advanced tools, or experimenting with AI, our goal is always the same: to make sure you feel heard, supported, and valued.

We’re constantly pushing the boundaries of customer support and always looking for ways to do better. Your feedback keeps us moving forward, and we’re excited to keep evolving and innovating!

Thanks for being part of the journey!
