Name: Navigating changes in direct debit: reducing failures
Post Body:
Why direct debit failure rates are a growing concern

Direct debit remains one of the most popular payment methods in the UK, underpinning everything from utility bills to subscription services. Yet the landscape is shifting, and not in businesses' favour. Direct debit failure rates have climbed sharply, squeezing cash flow and straining customer relationships at a time when neither can afford disruption.

The numbers tell a stark story. 2.7% of direct debit transactions failed in Q1 2025, up from 1.9% in Q1 2024 and just 1.3% pre-pandemic (FastPay). For businesses that rely on recurring payments, even small percentage increases translate into significant revenue leakage and administrative headaches.

Understanding what's driving these changes, and how to respond, is now essential for any business collecting payments via direct debit. This article breaks down the evolving landscape, the root causes of failure, and the practical strategies that reduce rejection rates.

What is changing in the direct debit landscape?

Several forces are reshaping how direct debits work in practice. Cost-of-living pressures have tightened household budgets, meaning more customers lack sufficient funds on collection day. At the same time, regulatory scrutiny around payment transparency has intensified. Customers now expect clearer advance notifications, flexible collection dates, and real-time visibility into upcoming charges.

The shift toward digital-first payment experiences also plays a role. Consumers are increasingly comfortable managing finances through apps and online portals. They expect to pause, modify, or cancel mandates instantly. This convenience, while positive for the customer, creates new operational challenges for businesses that haven't modernised their collection processes.

How are new customer behaviours affecting direct debit?

Today's customers demand flexibility and transparency around payment collection. They want to choose collection dates that align with their pay cycles. They expect SMS or email reminders before money leaves their account. And when something goes wrong, they want immediate, empathetic communication rather than a generic letter arriving days later.

The emotional dimension matters more than many businesses realise. 63% of adults feel stressed when a direct debit bounces, and 41% report avoiding contact with the provider afterward (FastPay). That avoidance delays resolution, makes debt recovery harder, and erodes trust. Businesses that fail to acknowledge this emotional burden risk losing customers who would otherwise stay.

Why do direct debit payments fail?

Reducing failures starts with understanding why they happen. The causes fall into a few well-defined categories, though their relative weight has shifted over the past few years.

Insufficient funds is by far the most common reason, representing more than 80% of failures. According to GoCardless transaction data across 55,000 UK customers and 52 million transactions, this single cause accounts for 2.38% of the average 2.9% failure rate (GoCardless). Cancelled mandates are the second most common reason, making up around 15% of failed payments.

Beyond these primary causes, failures also stem from incorrect or outdated account details, closed accounts, and technical processing errors. Each category requires a different response, which is why a blanket approach to failure management rarely works.

What role does data quality play in payment failures?

Poor data hygiene is a silent driver of preventable rejections. When customer records contain outdated bank details, incorrect sort codes, or mismatched account names, the payment fails before it even reaches the customer's bank. These aren't cases of insufficient funds. They're process failures that sit squarely within the business's control.

The problem compounds over time. Customers switch bank accounts, close old ones, or update details with one provider but not another. Without regular validation checks and automated account verification at the point of mandate setup, businesses accumulate stale data that generates avoidable failures month after month.

Certain sectors feel this pressure acutely. Electricity and gas direct debit failure rates more than doubled, climbing from 0.9% to over 2% in recent years, while financial services contend with failure rates between 2-4% (Access PaySuite). Much of this increase traces back to economic pressures, but outdated records amplify the problem.

How can businesses reduce direct debit failure rates?

The good news is that most direct debit failures are addressable. Businesses that take a proactive, multi-layered approach consistently outperform those relying on reactive measures alone. Here are the strategies that deliver the strongest results.

Pre-notification and advance communication. Sending clear reminders before collection, typically three to five days in advance, gives customers time to ensure funds are available. These notifications can be delivered via email, SMS, or even WhatsApp. The key is reaching customers on channels they actually use.

Smart retry logic. When a payment fails, the timing and frequency of retries matter enormously. Retrying too quickly risks hitting the same insufficient-funds problem. Waiting too long delays cash flow. Intelligent retry scheduling, often aligned to common payroll dates, recovers a meaningful share of initially failed payments. In 2024, 70% of all involuntary churn detected was recovered through automated retries and dunning campaigns (Churnkey).

Account validation at setup. Verifying bank details at the point of mandate creation eliminates a significant category of failures. Modulus checking, confirmation of payee, and real-time account validation tools catch errors before they enter your system.

Flexible collection dates. Offering customers a choice of collection date, such as the 1st, 15th, or last working day of the month, aligns payments with income patterns and reduces insufficient-funds rejections.

What operational changes make the biggest impact?

Beyond individual tactics, systemic operational improvements drive lasting results. Monitoring failure analytics is a critical first step. Businesses should track failure rates by reason code, customer segment, and collection date. This data reveals patterns, such as higher failure rates on specific dates or among certain customer cohorts, that inform targeted interventions.

Working with payment platforms that offer built-in automation also makes a significant difference. Adfin, for example, supports multiple payment methods including direct debits, cards, and open banking, while automating payment chasing across email, WhatsApp, and SMS. This multi-channel approach helps businesses recover failed payments faster without manual follow-up.

The broader trend is clear. Half of all companies view declined payments as a major cause of customer churn, and top-performing businesses are 12 times more likely to use specialised third-party payment recovery software (Merchant Risk Council). Investing in the right tools isn't optional anymore. It's a competitive necessity.

The annual trajectory confirms the urgency. The UK direct debit failure rate was 12% higher in August 2024 compared to August 2023 (Mortgage Finance Gazette). Businesses that delay action will face compounding losses as failure rates continue to climb.

FAQs

What is a typical direct debit failure rate?

Pre-pandemic, the average UK direct debit failure rate sat around 1.3%. By Q1 2025, that figure had risen to 2.7%. Industry-specific rates vary considerably. Utilities and energy providers see rates around 2%, while financial services can experience 2-4%. A rate consistently below 2% is generally considered healthy for most sectors.

Can failed direct debits be automatically retried?

Yes. Most payment processors and bureau services support automatic retries. Best practice is to schedule the first retry three to five business days after the initial failure, ideally around common salary payment dates. Dunning emails and SMS alone achieve an average recovery rate of 42%, making automated follow-up one of the most effective tools available.

How do direct debit failures affect customer retention?

The impact is substantial. Studies show that 20-40% of churn for subscription-based businesses is involuntary, driven by failed payments rather than a customer's active decision to cancel (FlyCode). Customers who experience a bounced payment often feel embarrassed and avoid engaging with the business, making proactive outreach essential.

How far in advance should customers be notified before collection?

The Direct Debit Guarantee requires advance notice of collection amounts and dates. Best practice is to notify customers at least three to five working days before the collection date. This gives them time to ensure funds are available and reduces insufficient-funds failures significantly.

What payment methods complement direct debit to reduce risk?

Offering alternative payment methods alongside direct debit gives customers flexibility and reduces dependency on a single channel. Cards, open banking, and bank transfers each serve different customer preferences. Platforms like Adfin allow businesses to accept all these methods through a single interface, making it easier to offer choice without adding operational complexity.

How can small businesses afford payment recovery tools?

Many modern payment platforms charge per successful transaction rather than imposing monthly fees. This pay-for-performance model means small businesses only pay when collections succeed, removing the upfront cost barrier. Adfin's transparent pricing model follows exactly this approach, aligning its costs with your collection outcomes.

What is the fastest way to identify why payments are failing?

Analyse failure reason codes provided by your payment processor or bureau. Group failures by category (insufficient funds, cancelled mandates, invalid details) and by collection date. This segmentation quickly reveals whether the issue is economic, data-related, or process-driven, allowing you to target the right fix.

Moving forward with confidence

Rising direct debit failure rates aren't inevitable. They're a signal that collection strategies need to evolve. The businesses that thrive will combine better data management, smarter retry logic, proactive customer communication, and flexible payment options into a cohesive approach.

Technology plays a central role in this evolution. Automated chasing, real-time account validation, and multi-channel payment acceptance aren't luxuries. They're the foundation of reliable cash flow in a landscape where customer expectations and economic conditions continue to shift. The sooner businesses adapt, the stronger their collections and customer relationships will be.

Name: Neil Criddle: betting on Adfin early
Post Body:
"For credit control, Adfin is on another level—clear, flexible, and built for accountants."

When it comes to early adopters, Neil Criddle might just take the title. As the founder of Neil’s Data Consultancy, Neil was one of the first to sign up with Adfin - even before our direct debit functionality had officially launched. That kind of trust isn’t something we take lightly.

In this week’s spotlight, Neil shares how he built a business that blends data consultancy with accounting, why he took a chance on Adfin early on, and how streamlining payments has helped him deliver a better experience for his clients.

Can you tell me a little bit about you and your company?

I spent about 12 years in commercial finance with big corporate businesses. Most of my time was focused on taking numbers and communicating them in a way people could understand. That’s really where my passion lies.

I was made redundant multiple times, and after the last time in January 2020, I decided enough was enough. I started my own business, doing something similar to what I did before but leaning more into traditional accountancy - things like tax returns and bookkeeping.

Two months later, COVID hit. We had no money, no clients, and I had to homeschool the kids…but we grew pretty quickly over 2020 and 2021 by offering support around things like the furlough scheme. People really needed help.

By the end of 2021, we started building a team. Fast forward to now, and just over five years later, we’ve grown to a team of 12 with around 650 clients. We're based just outside Bristol, in Weston-super-Mare. It’s been rapid growth, and we’re having a great time.

Do you work with any particular clients or serve specific industries?

We serve all sorts of clients, but the businesses we work best with are owned by people who are ambitious, entrepreneurial, and really want to grow. That mindset aligns with ours.

How would you describe your dream client?

Ideally, it’s someone who’s not interested in the back-office financial admin. They’re happy for us to just get on with it and they value what we do. On top of that, they want to grow. That’s where we come in - not just doing their bookkeeping and tax returns, but also helping with management reports, budgeting, forecasting, and acting as a trusted advisor. We’re not just someone they speak to once a year at tax time.

How do you differentiate yourself from other accountancy firms?

It’s definitely our consulting focus, thanks to my background. Locally, we do a lot of business advisory work - helping people actually understand their numbers, not just handing them a tax return and a bill.

But I think our biggest differentiator is our marketing. We have a strong social media presence. Most accountants either don’t do social media or don’t do it well. During lockdown, I had to build the business online because we couldn’t go anywhere. That gave us a major edge.

How has LinkedIn and social media shaped your business growth? Were there any challenges?

Social media has definitely created more opportunities. The challenges have mostly come from trying to manage the rapid growth. But, being active online helped me connect with so many people. I’m friends with people like you - the team at Adfin, folks at Xero. I now coach on behalf of an academy I started learning through at the beginning. The owner saw my journey through what I posted online, and now I get to go to Portugal twice a year to work with them. These opportunities wouldn’t have happened if I just delivered great service but didn’t talk about it online.

We have clients all over the country. I go to London five or six times a year to meet them, all because of the visibility we've built online.

Do you have any advice for founders or business owners trying to grow their visibility online?

Surround yourself with people who get it - not just revenue drivers, but peers in your industry. I’ve got a great circle of accountants I talk to regularly. We’re not in competition; we want to help each other grow. That’s been a big part of building my business - sharing, networking, and being part of that community.

Do you have any fun facts about your journey or about yourself?

We sponsor a couple of professional darts players - one of them is also a client and currently in the top 10 in the world. So if you follow darts, you might recognise him.

Another fun fact: I spoke at Xerocon last year, which was a huge milestone for me. And I’ve mentioned the work I do with the academy - when I go to Portugal I get to meet people from the US, Canada, South Africa. It’s amazing to get all those folks in one place. It’s inspiring to be part of that kind of network.

Do you have a moment in your business journey that you're especially proud of? A point where you felt like you'd made it?

Buying our forever home. It’s everything I’d dreamed of - a lovely garden, a swimming pool, loads of space, and it’s out in the countryside. The kids love it, the dog loves it, and my wife adores the kitchen with the island. That’s when I stopped to reflect and thought, “We’ve actually done all right.”

Speaking at Xerocon was another big moment. That kind of recognition was huge. Xero even sponsors some of our workwear now. And on the tech side, we were the very first UK accountancy firm to use Adfin’s direct debit functionality. I actually signed the agreement before it was even live, back in July last year. That’s a fun fact not many people know.

We’ve also acquired a couple of accountancy firms in the past year, which is something I wouldn’t have imagined doing even two or three years ago. And now, five years in, we’re the highest-rated firm in our town on Google - beating out companies that have been around for 30 or 40 years. So yeah, those are the big milestones for me: the house, Xerocon, and our Google rating.

What drove you to start using Adfin? 

We were reshuffling our tech stack and moving away from a platform that handled both proposals and direct debits. So we needed two replacements. I already had a proposal tool lined up - my friend Jonathan in Bristol was building one, and I knew I’d use it.

When it came to finding a payments provider, I hadn’t done much research because our old tool covered it. I was looking at GoCardless when a friend, Jordan, messaged me on LinkedIn. He suggested jumping on a call with a new company - Adfin - for some market research.

I hopped on a Zoom call with Tom, Sam, and Ciprian. They were just getting started and couldn’t do direct debits yet, but I really liked their roadmap and ethos. The platform was new, but I felt like we could help shape it. It was a bit of a leap, but I was excited about being part of something from the ground up. We signed up pretty much straight away.

Is there one particular feature of Adfin that you find most valuable?

It changes month to month as they keep developing. Right now, it’s the credit control functionality. We’ve restructured internally and created an ops team, and one of their responsibilities is credit control.

Once all our legacy invoicing is phased out, everything will be run through Adfin. The dashboard is really clean, easy to understand, and allows for filtering and tagging, which helps a lot. We don’t have a massive credit control issue, but as we’ve grown, 10% of a bigger number becomes a more serious issue. Adfin handles that far better than pulling reports from Xero.

They’re also natively integrating with Socket, our proposal tool, which was a lucky coincidence. We're doing some beta testing with them now, helping refine that integration.

Are there any tech trends or other tools you’re particularly excited about?

Definitely. Socket has only been around for about a year, but we’ve been involved in its roadmap, and they’re doing great work. Another one is our practice management system, Engager, which was also built by an accountancy practice owner. He really understands the challenges we face, and it’s been brilliant for workflow.

We’re also looking at implementing Active Workpapers. Since we acquired a couple of firms last year, we’ve got a lot of new team members and clients. This tool should help standardise our working paper processes moving forward.

If you could automate anything in your life, what would it be?

Definitely my email inbox. I get over 100 emails a day, and when I’m offsite it gets out of control fast. I’d love an AI that could filter and respond intelligently.

What’s your go-to drink while working? And while not working?

Water during work hours, cider after (class west country choice!). Though a recent trip to Portugal converted me to neat spirits - age changes things!

Name: Nicola Hageman swapped faceless tools for support that listens
Post Body:
"Your support team is incredible. If something goes wrong, you get an answer within an hour... that’s so rare and so valuable."

We’re proud to spotlight Nicola - one of our loveliest customers (and brave enough to share a stage with us!).

Now the founder of The Numbers Quarter and co-creator of FreshPay, she shares her story of building two businesses, supporting women in business, and why customer support matters most.

How did you get into accounting?

I’ve wanted to be an accountant since I was about eight years old - which sounds a bit sad! But my brother had a friend who lived in a big house with a secret doorway to another room, and his mum was an accountant. So, in my head, I thought, “I want a big house with a secret room. I’m going to be an accountant!”

Turns out the dad was also a big-shot lawyer in London, so that probably explained the house. But still, that kind of kickstarted it. I’ve always loved maths, numbers, logical things - and I’ve always been a bit of a Del Boy. My friends actually called me Del Boy at uni. I was always starting something new - party planning, MLM stuff - you name it. I just really enjoy business.

I started out working in an IT company in London, where I got most of my training - management accounts, commercial management, working with big train operating companies. I loved it. I used to work on big bids and financials, spending my days building massive spreadsheets (which I loved).

Ten years ago, I started my practice - The Numbers Quarter. It was originally just called Nicola Hageman Accountancy because I do numbers, not creative branding!

What do you specialise in at The Numbers Quarter?

We’ve found ourselves working with a lot of female business owners recently, which I love. We’re also an all-female team, which is really special. I think running a business as a woman - and particularly as a mum - is just different.

I hate the term mumpreneur because it really downplays the work involved, but there is a unique dynamic. Men often have someone at home supporting them, so they go all in - 60-hour weeks, weekends, the works. That first year, they scale quickly.

Women, on the other hand, often start businesses for flexibility - school pickups, caring for elderly relatives. So growth isn’t always fast out the gate. I started in exactly the same position. It helps to work with clients who relate to that reality. I can say to them: don’t compare yourself to others - your path is different, and that’s okay.

If you could describe a dream client, what would they be like?

They’ve got to be nice. That’s a must. If someone’s respectful and kind, we’re happy. But beyond that, our ideal client is someone who’s been winging it for a few years, doing well, and now realises, “Hey, this could be something bigger.” They want clarity - they want to stop stressing about tax bills and cash flow. That’s when we step in and take those worries off their hands so they can focus on what they’re best at.

Are there new tech developments that have changed the way you run things?

Yes - I love tech. I’m a bit of a geek. I always want to try new tools, much to my team’s dismay! I get shiny object syndrome and want to test everything. AI especially is really exciting. ChatGPT is basically my new best friend. It’s so polite and encouraging - it’s like a personal cheerleader! I use it all the time.

I’ve heard about some AI tools being planned for our industry, and I can’t wait to try them out. That kind of innovation makes everything smoother and more efficient.

What’s been your proudest moment so far in your career or business journey?

Still genuinely enjoying what I do and being excited for the future of The Numbers Quarter - even 10 years in. That, and I’m also one of the founders of FreshPay, which I’m incredibly proud of. This new tax year has been phenomenal for us. Seeing other accountants say how good your software is - that’s an amazing feeling. When someone recommends it, it’s like: yes! We did that.

Tell me about FreshPay! What is it, and how did it start?

About four years ago, I posted in an accountancy group asking for recommendations for cloud-based payroll software. No one had anything solid. Two people I’d never spoken to before commented with a throwaway line: “Why don’t we just build one?”

So we did. FreshPay was born. It’s all self-funded. We had a few early testers who invested a bit, but otherwise it’s all been done by us. We’re all accountants and payroll bureaus ourselves, so we designed the software to make our lives easier - automations, clarity, efficiency. That then helps our clients, too.

What makes FreshPay stand out?

It’s built specifically for bureaus, so it’s full of efficiencies that make payroll more profitable for the person running it. It’s all about usability and support. We’ve built it from our own pain points, and that really shows.

What made you decide to start using Adfin?

I met Tom and Sam at Accountex North last October. I’d never heard of Adfin before, but I went over for a chat because it sounded interesting - like a better alternative to GoCardless. They were just such lovely people, and I’m a people person. GoCardless always felt faceless to me. So I gave Adfin a try and moved all our clients over. We’ve had a few teething issues, but we love it, and the support’s been brilliant.

Is there a particular Adfin feature you find most valuable?

The ability to track customer status - like who hasn’t signed a mandate and what stage each invoice is at - is really helpful. I also love that a link to pay by card is automatically sent out if a direct debit fails so you know it's being sorted! You can focus your attention where it’s actually needed, instead of chasing your tail.

Also, your support team is incredible. If something goes wrong, you get an answer within an hour. That’s so rare and so valuable. Honestly, that’s probably the biggest differentiator.

What’s your go-to drink while working?

Coffee - a latte. I actually bought a proper coffee machine for the office. It’s bean-to-cup, and I use Wonky Coffee, which I love. They save the beans and create a sustainable blend.

And your go-to drink when you’re not working?

I love prosecco, but I’m often the one driving or trying not to be hungover for days, because I’m too old for that now! So I often opt for the non-alcoholic version.

Post Body:
"I love being able to see everything in one place - all the clients, all the payments coming through, and who they relate to. With Adfin, it’s all clear and user-friendly."

In the spotlight this week is Nicola, the founder of Accounts and Tax Made Easy. Nicola shares how a career pivot led to launching her own practice, why she’s a proud generalist with a soft spot for service businesses, and how Adfin helped her ditch one-off invoices for a streamlined, scalable system.

So! Tell us about you - how did you get into accounting?

I left school wanting to be a mechanic but my second choice was accounting and went straight into it. I did take a year out, lived in Spain, worked in bars and factories - basically any job that gave me money to do what I wanted. Then I went to full-time college and I just loved it. I love accounts. I love the way it reconciles, just making things work and sorting things out. I've done it since I was about 17 or 18.

I’ve always had a few clients on the side, probably for the last ten years or so. In 2003, I got made redundant. I took a month off and then started this business, Accounts and Tax Made Easy. This is my baby, and I really want to grow it.

What kind of clients do you usually work with?

I don’t have a specific niche like a lot of accountancy practices do. I like that our clients are all totally different. But we do niche down on personality — we have to get on with our clients. We focus on working with people who value us, want to grow their businesses, and want us to be part of that journey.

I heard someone say their niche is being a “proud generalist,” and I loved that, I really enjoy the variety.

And in terms of industries, are there certain types of businesses where you feel you bring the most value?

I love working with service-based businesses, especially one-man bands who want to grow, and I’ve got some larger warehouse and e-commerce clients too. That’s where I bring in my business advisory work.

Warehousing can be chaotic (no offense!): they’re often just focused on getting orders out the door. But with my Efficiency and Profit Framework, we take a step back, set proper goals, and make real progress. So in a way, I’ve got two sides: the advisory side for bigger warehouse clients, and more traditional accounting for service-based businesses. I love the variety – every day feels different.

What moments have shaped your journey the most?

I’ve always landed the jobs I wanted – maybe I’m good at interviews, or just good at the job! I moved up quickly, but the last five years have been the hardest.

After having my son, I was told to come back to work a week after giving birth. I refused – and was forced to leave the job. My confidence took a hit, and I went back to bookkeeping, even though I was nearly qualified. But I rebuilt from there.

During COVID, I helped buy a company out of administration, turned it around, and sold it for seven figures. That’s what led me into business advisory.

I passed all 17 ACCA exams but realised the corporate world wasn’t for me. I wanted to work with real people, so I went back to AAT and set up on my own. Running your own business has its challenges – but I wouldn’t trade it.

What does your dream client look like?

Honestly? Someone whose accounts are in a complete mess, and they know and want help! I had one client who only had sales invoices for two whole years… nothing else. That kind of chaos doesn’t scare me.

But personality is just as important. I want to work with people I can have a proper chat with, not just awkward, transactional meetings. And trust is huge. They’ve got to trust me to step in and sort things out, which isn’t always easy when it comes to money and I have to trust they will put in the work and actions we create together.

The real dream clients are the ones who want to improve. It’s not just about fixing things once, it’s about working together to make lasting changes. That’s where the magic happens.

What first drew you to Adfin?

All my clients were on a pay-as-you-go basis, especially for self-assessment. I’d have to chase and chase, not hear anything, send an invoice, and say, “Until you pay, I’m not doing it.” It was a bit of a pain. I wanted to switch to direct debits.

I tried GoCardless but only managed to get about three clients on it - it just wasn’t easy to set up. I didn’t find it intuitive. Then I found out about Adfin and moved all my self-assessment clients onto monthly direct debits. Now I do the invoices in Xero, and Adfin sends them out. It’s just so much easier. They even chase when the mandate needs signing for new clients!

Is there a particular Adfin feature you find most valuable?

Definitely the online portal. I love being able to see everything in one place - all the clients, all the payments coming through, and who they relate to. With Adfin, it’s all clear and user-friendly.

If you could automate anything in your life, what would it be?

Oh my goodness, the washing! Definitely the washing. It’s not even difficult… it just never ends. There’s only three of us in the house and I have no idea where it all comes from!

For work, I’d automate the mailbox. The inbox never clears. We try to stay on top of it -  I check in the morning, my admin lady checks in the afternoon - but it’s relentless.

What’s one task you love doing, and one you’d happily never do again?

I love doing a set of accounts on Excel. No Xero, no software - just old-school spreadsheets. Sifting through PDFs and bank statements, building it manually. It makes me feel like a “real” accountant again.

One I’d happily never do again? Onboarding. There are so many boxes to tick - forms, ID checks, getting the client fully set up. It’s never made easy for us or the client. Everyone I speak to says the same, which is why I’ve now got a dedicated person to handle it.

What’s your go-to drink while working?

Black coffee in the morning, then it’s water for the rest of the day. Nothing exciting, I’m afraid!

What about your go-to drink when you’re not working?

On the weekend? I love a glass of champagne - I’m such a snob! Champagne or a nice white wine.

Name: On call at Adfin: how we keep things running smoothly
Post Body:
At Adfin, we help businesses get paid faster and take the hassle out of credit control. That means our systems need to be available and responsive around the clock because invoices are sent, payments are received, and cash flow is chased at all hours of the day. 

We want to offer the best possible service to our customers, but every software has issues and bugs. Therefore, we aim to identify and fix any issues before our users even notice them - and if they do notice and report an issue, our definition of awesome is saying that “Thanks for reporting it, we’ve already identified it and the team is shipping a fix right now”. 

This post is a behind-the-scenes look at how we handle on-call, ensuring we're always ready to respond to issues and keep everything running smoothly, day or night. It is written to be digestible for all levels, whether you're an engineer or someone simply curious about how we stay online 24/7. 

What it means to be on‑call

At Adfin, our backend engineers rotate weekly in the on‑call guardian role. This means being ready to respond to incoming alerts, whether it’s a sudden spike in errors, a failed payout, or a customer flagging something that doesn’t look right. We subscribe to the “you build it, you run it” mindset, meaning that those who write the code support it in production. This creates tight feedback loops, faster resolution times, and a strong sense of ownership across the team.

How incidents reach us

When something goes wrong in our systems, like a payment not going through or a screen not loading properly, we rely on a few key tools to help us spot and fix it quickly.

Every time our software does something, it leaves a digital trail called a log. These logs give us an audit of what was happening under the hood, such as whether an action was successful or not. We collect and monitor these logs using Datadog, which gives us a real-time view into the health of our systems. It works much like a car dashboard, showing us warning signs, performance metrics, and unusual activity so we can spot and respond to issues before they turn into bigger problems.

When Datadog detects an issue, it automatically raises an alert through incident.io, which we use to manage and respond to incidents.  incident.io is our incident management tool. It creates a central place for us to respond to issues when things go wrong. It tells us who’s on call, what needs to be investigated, and gives us a running timeline of everything that’s happened. Because it connects directly to Slack, we can coordinate our response in real time, without switching between tools. That means less confusion, faster resolutions, and a clear record of what happened and how we fixed it. Having everything in Slack, from assigning ownership to sharing updates, keeps the entire team in the loop and helps us move quickly when things go wrong.

Even if the problem only affects one customer or seems minor, we take it seriously. We dig in, figure out what went wrong, and fix it properly so it doesn’t happen again.

What happens during an incident

Every incident is different, but there are some typical steps we follow to make sure we stay calm, respond quickly, and resolve things properly.

When an incident is raised, the on-call guardian acknowledges it in incident.io, which lets the team know someone is on it.

We then begin to investigate. This means diving into logs and metrics, checking what the system was doing at the time, and looking at recent changes or related issues. Our aim is to identify the root cause, not just the surface error.

Next, we try to understand the impact. Is this affecting just one customer or many? Is money movement involved? Are downstream systems affected? Knowing the scope helps us decide how urgent the response needs to be.

Throughout the process, we communicate in Slack. Thanks to incident.io, there’s a dedicated Slack channel per incident where we share updates and coordinate the response. The on-call guardian is typically the incident lead, but in certain cases, the right people need to be involved and the incident lead could be assigned to someone else.

If we find a straightforward, safe solution, we’ll often apply a hotfix. This is a small, focused code change that can be deployed immediately, rather than waiting for the next scheduled release. This helps us fix urgent issues fast without compromising stability.

Finally, once everything is back to normal, we close the incident. We write a short summary on what happened, what we did to resolve it, and whether any long-term changes are needed. In more serious cases, we’ll do a post-incident review so the whole team can learn from what happened.

It’s not a rigid process as every incident is unique, but having this structure helps us stay organised and responsive, even when things go wrong unexpectedly.

How we prevent issues from reaching production

Each backend engineer takes a one‑week on‑call shift. In the week before their shift, they act as the Dev Guardian, with a focus on preventing issues before they reach customers.

We work across three environments: dev, staging, and production. Dev is used for everyday coding and early testing, staging is our pre-production test environment that is also used by our platform integrations, while production is our live system.

The Dev Guardian reviews both the dev and staging environments for errors or unusual activity, and shares anything suspicious with the team. They assign owners to issues that need fixing, so bugs are dealt with before we release them to production. They're also in charge of checking our end-to-end (E2E) test results. These are automated tests that simulate how a real user would interact with the product. These tests are crucial for catching unexpected issues, and the Dev Guardian ensures they're running smoothly and highlighting any genuine problems.

This early focus on quality helps us keep production stable and our customers happy.

Release cadence

We release new changes once a week, and the on-call shift is timed to support this cycle.

On Monday, the on-call guardian starts their shift by preparing the system for release. This includes a brief code freeze (a pause on merging new changes) to make sure we’re testing a stable version of our product. They then perform a regression test of our key flows, checking that core features such as invoice creation and payments are working as expected.

Once everything looks good, we deploy to staging, our pre-production environment. This gives us a final opportunity to catch bugs or regressions before promoting to production on Tuesday, when the release goes live for customers.

Why this works

What sets Adfin apart is how much effort we put into preventing issues before they happen.

  • Proactive mindset: We don’t wait for incidents to escalate. We treat every exception, failed test, or minor complaint as a signal worth investigating. This helps us catch problems early and fix them before they affect customers.
  • Structured ownership: Our rotating Dev Guardian and On-Call Guardian roles give each engineer dedicated time to focus on quality and stability. Just as importantly, they offer exposure to the full platform. Every engineer gets hands-on experience across all parts of the system, building a deep understanding of how everything fits together. 
  • Built-in escalation: By using incident.io and Slack together, we can respond to problems quickly and clearly, without confusion or duplicated effort.
  • Disciplined releases: Our weekly release rhythm, with staging checks, manual tests, and hotfix options, gives us confidence that what we ship is safe and reliable.

In summary

Keeping the lights on at Adfin isn’t just about reacting to fires. It’s about building systems, habits, and culture that make fires less likely in the first place. We work together, share what we learn, and treat reliability as something we all own.

At Adfin, we care deeply about delivering the best possible experience for our customers. That means every alert, test failure, and minor issue gets our attention.

Name: One year at Adfin: becoming a builder
Post Body:
🎉 One Year at Adfin: Becoming a Builder

One year ago, I leaped.

I felt stuck, creatively bored, and professionally underwhelmed at the time in my previous job. So when the opportunity to join a small group of passionate minds working on something bold came along, I didn’t hesitate (too much).

🚀 Joining a dream that was still in draft

When I joined Adfin, it wasn’t quite the company you see today. Back then, it felt more like a concept taking shape, with just a few determined people trying to bring to life the only platform that automates the end-to-end process of getting paid.

I was the first software engineer to join the team, outside of the founding members, essentially the first employee. That meant I wasn’t just another new hire; I was stepping into a pivotal role to help build the engineering foundation and turn big ideas into working realities.

What gave me confidence was the founding team itself. These weren’t just any colleagues; they were people I had worked with before, and deeply respected for their talent, clarity, and collaborative spirit. Their belief in this idea made it easy to believe in it too.

I knew it was a startup. I knew that meant risk.
But what I didn’t know was just how big the challenge and the growth would be.

🌀 My workflows crash course

When I joined Adfin, I had no background in workflows honestly, I didn’t even know what a workflow engine did. Concepts like orchestration, BPMN, or async execution weren’t on my radar. But suddenly, they were my responsibility.

That’s when I met our tool of choice for orchestrating processes. I dove in headfirst, reading, experimenting, asking questions, breaking things (and fixing them). It was intense, but incredibly rewarding.

Within the first month, we had a fully functional workflow in place, one that could autonomously schedule tasks and send notifications. Looking back, it’s still wild to me how fast that came together, especially considering how unfamiliar it all was on day one.

🧠 From unknowns to ownership

Workflows quickly became my main focus, and what a deep, fascinating world I had stepped into.

I had never owned a project with so many moving parts and unknowns. Every day brought something new to figure out:

  • Asynchronous job execution and scheduling

  • Transactional boundaries and propagation in relational databases

  • Design and orchestration of process definitions using BPMN engines

None of it was familiar. All of it had to be built from scratch. But challenge by challenge, line by line, I was learning. Some days felt like steady progress. Others felt like creative chaos, in the best way.

Along the way, my Java skills sharpened, my technical confidence grew, and my mindset shifted from “I need to figure this out” to “I can build this.” This wasn’t just about shipping a feature; it was about designing a system from the ground up that would become a cornerstone of our product.

🤝 The people who made it worth it

As a team, we’ve been through ups and downs, as has Adfin. We’ve faced our share of challenges, no doubt but we made it through them together.

Yes, there were long working days. Yes, there were weekends away from family. But through it all, it always felt worth it because I believed in what we were building, and even more, I believed in who I was building it with.

I’ve learned something from each of my colleagues every single day. And I want to give some special shout-outs:

  • To Ciprian, for believing in me from day one, giving me space to grow, and always being there to listen even when things got messy.
  • To Andra and Silviu, for their unwavering patience, true camaraderie, and constant readiness to jump in, guide, and support, no matter how busy things got.
  • And Florin, who somehow knows everything, always has the answer to even my most complicated questions and never makes me feel silly for asking the simple ones.

It’s a rare thing to be surrounded by people who lift you, challenge you, and support you at the same time. I don’t take that for granted.

🏁 One year in and still running

A year later, I’m still running that marathon. The team has grown. The product is real. The mission is clear. And me? I’ve gone from cautiously curious to fully committed.

It hasn’t always been easy. But it has always been worth it.

I’m proud of what we’ve built. I’m grateful for the trust the team placed in me. And I’m excited (and maybe a little nervous in the best way) to see what Year Two has in store.

So here’s to a year of growth, grit, and great people.
And to the next phase of the journey, whatever workflows it brings. 😉

Name: Payments chaos to payments calm: how Adfin puts all your payment tools in one place
Post Body:
When we first founded Adfin, we quickly realised that accountants and small businesses were in payment tool hell. A typical accounting firm was using GoCardless for direct debit, Worldpay or Stripe for cards, Crezco for open banking, and still manually tracking bank transfers. We knew there was a better way - so we set out to build a single platform that could do it all.

What Adfin brought together first

Direct debit

The bread and butter of recurring client payments - reliable, flexible and a smooth client experience (we wrote a lot more on why we think it’s so great here). We built our direct debit offering with easy mandate setup and tracking, configurable retries (with no charges for failures) and smart fallbacks.

Many businesses were already using a direct debit provider, but were frustrated with the lack of flexibility or poor support. So we built mandate migration, enabling businesses to transfer to Adfin without clients needing to sign new mandates - so no interruptions to client collections, and no paperwork.

‍

Cards (including Apple Pay & Google Pay)

Great for one-off and urgent payments, like yearly self-assessment clients. With support for Apple Pay and Google Pay, your clients can pay you from their mobiles in a matter of seconds - so now there’s no excuse! 

“One-time payments and Apple Pay are brilliant - especially for the year-end clients who only get one invoice a year.”

Louise Moore, Moore to Bookkeeping

‍

Pay by bank 

Account to account payments without the pain of manual data entry - clients pick their bank and pay directly from their banking app. 


All the other smart stuff that makes it feel joined‑up

The payment itself is only one piece of the puzzle - we also built; 

  • Payment limits to cap fees and help to steer payers to your preferred, lower-cost payment methods
  • Automatic reminders & chasing that stop the moment your client makes a payment 
  • Daily payouts with instant reconciliation to your accounting software (Xero and Quickbooks) 
  • Branded pages & emails to keep your brand front and centre 

All that good stuff meant firms like Helpbox were able to consolidate 4 payment tools into 1, simplifying their operations and saving them 58% on their payment collection costs.

But we knew that we could do more! 

What’s new: Adfin is now truly end‑to‑end

Instalment plans 

Spread a client’s payments over time without additional admin. 

We’ve built instalment plans with fully configurable frequencies and amounts, the option to collect On Demand or with Auto Collect, and automatic updates against the planned invoice (no need to manually allocate payments). Read more about how our instalment plans work here. 

Bank transfers (with automated reconciliation) 

At last! Now you can accept bank transfers directly from the Adfin payment page. 

We’ll show your client intermediary bank details - then when a client makes a payment, we automatically detect and update it. No checking or chasing needed after the money lands, and no more need for you to manually ‘mark as paid’ in your accounting software. 

Statements (coming soon!)

A single source of truth for outstanding payments and invoices, which your clients can pay in a single payment link. 

The end result

Now Adfin can be your single collections tool from request to reconciliation, with clients able to pay any way that they choose. 

Book a demo or get in touch with our team to get started with Adfin.

Name: Say hello to Adfin bank transfer: a smarter way to get paid
Post Body:
Bank transfers have been stuck in the past

Bank transfers are one of the most popular ways for businesses to get paid, but they weren't built for modern business processes.

You send your invoice, check your bank for the payment, double-check references, and manually match what’s come in with what’s still outstanding. If there's been an overpayment you need to manually create an entry on your accounting software. If there's been an underpayment you need to chase your client to pay again.

With Adfin bank transfers, that’s all handled for you. Clients can now pay directly by bank transfer through your Adfin payment link, and each payment is automatically matched.

Making bank transfers fit for the digital world

We've built Adfin bank transfers to give you all the benefits of digital payments — instant visibility, automatic reconciliation, and reduced admin — but at a lower cost and to fit with your clients' existing payable processes.

Here’s how they make life easier:

  • Automatic payment allocation so you never waste time figuring out which payment belongs to which invoice
  • No more double chasing: Adfin detects payments as soon as they’re made, so you don’t follow up on invoices that are already paid
  • Real-time posting to your accounting software, keeping Xero or QuickBooks fully up to date
  • Lower processing costs than other digital payments like cards, with the same reliability and visibility
  • A seamless experience for your clients, who can pay straight from their bank with no extra steps

Adfin bank transfers use unique bank account details for each client, meaning that you don't have to expose your account information externally either.

How Adfin bank transfers work

When a client chooses to pay using Adfin bank transfer through your Adfin payment link, they’re shown bank details for an intermediary clearing account that’s linked to your business. Once they send the payment, Adfin automatically matches it to the right invoice or payment request:

  • If the payment reference matches an invoice or request number, it’s allocated straight away
  • If the client pays too little, Adfin records a partial payment, we then continue chasing the client for the outstanding amount automatically
  • If they pay too much, Adfin creates an overpayment entry and alerts you by email
  • If no match is found, Adfin uses the payment amount or the most overdue invoice to allocate it automatically

Everything is then posted directly to your connected accounting software, so your books and your bank feed stay in sync.

Settlements and controls made simple

Funds from Adfin bank transfers are paid out to your bank account alongside your card and direct debit settlements.

You’re fully in control of how bank transfers work for your business. From the console, you can:

  • Set minimum and maximum payment limits for your account
  • Customise these limits for each client

Get started

Your account will automatically be enabled with Adfin bank transfer. In some cases, you may need to confirm your business details — we'll send you a notification in the console if this is the case.

New to Adfin? Book a demo or chat with our team, we’ll show you how Adfin bank transfers work and how they can save you hours of reconciliation time each week. Learn more at adfin.com.

Name: Smoother, smarter, sleeker: Adfin’s ongoing UI evolution
Post Body:
Adfin has been rapidly growing in the past months. The entirety of it is the grace of both fantastic management and engineering. Today we will talk about our frontend engineering team at Adfin.

Introduction

What makes building the user interface for our platform unique is the rapid pace of product change and development. Time to market is critical. At the same time, Product Quality and User Experience are non-negotiable at Adfin. We don’t cut corners.

As a result, our frontend engineers must carefully balance speed with the right level of effort when building new features and interfaces.

Diving deeper

So, how do we actually achieve that? Teamwork plays a significant role in our success, and our approach is closely aligned with DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) principles: we place a strong emphasis on minimising lead times and increasing deployment frequency, whilst maintaining the reliability of our product and reducing mean time to restore when incidents occur.

Most crucially, this is only possible with the support of our management team at Adfin. Championing a culture of autonomy and ownership, our management team enables engineers to work in the way top performers in our industry should operate.

For example, when it comes to writing code (more specifically building our React components), we always choose to create reusable components. Rather than reaching for overly abstract or generic components that attempt to solve multiple use cases at once, we prioritise simplicity. This allows us to keep our codebase maintainable, reduce duplication, and make future changes faster and safer.

Concrete example

Over the past few months, Adfin has quickly evolved from using slightly modified Material components, which bundled both logic and styling, to building its own components using headless solutions with a proprietary look and feel.

One such migration is our table component, which was recently launched into the live environment in our last release.

The story of our previous table started on August 13th, 2024. At the time it was built entirely with Material UI’s Data Grid component only. We managed to keep it live until a few days ago, when we decided to rebuild it with TanStack’s Table, in order to support resizeable columns and sub-rows for our upcoming payouts dashboard updates.

Having rebuilt the table ourselves, I can personally say that building a table is hard.

Would this have been feasible back in August 2024? Not really. As Adfin was growing fast, we were releasing new features every week (and I mean, full-fledged features, not just a new modal or input here and there).

And… would Adfin have needed a custom table at the time? Not at all, and it is why it’s only now, almost a year later that we’ve built it. Once again, time to market is critical, and building a table component would have taken one of our engineers 1–2 weeks (instead of launching at least two full features in the same timeframe!).

Wrap up!

Our intentional focus on keeping things simple is driven by the fact that we’re operating in a rapidly evolving environment. Our components are designed to solve today’s needs, not hypothetical ones. However, if an engineer can anticipate future use cases without adding significant complexity, they’re encouraged to account for it and implement it. Conversely, if the win is very small, and the effort is very large, we will not do it.

Clear, pragmatic code wins every time. Timing is key for Adfin, and we’re going to keep employing strategic choices in our product development cycle.

Name: Still early. Still learning.
Post Body:
Still Early. Still Learning

It’s been just over a year since I joined a magnificent team to bring Invoxx to life (Adfin’s original name, thank goodness we changed it!).

I’ve been here since day one. Not writing code, but trying to figure out the product we needed to build to get our first customers on board. That meant demos, feedback calls, follow-ups, chasing leads, and doing whatever it took to move things forward. My role has always focused on go-to-market (GTM) and on helping build the commercial side of the business. In the past year, I’ve done over 500 demos plus plenty more feedback calls.

So yeah, I’ve explained what Adfin is more times than I can count. But I’ve also listened. A lot. To the reality of how accountants and bookkeepers actually deal with getting paid.

This post isn’t about how we cracked it. It’s just a few honest reflections on what I’ve learned so far, what’s resonated, what I’ve seen firsthand, and why I’ve come to really enjoy working with this industry.

‍

Why the simple stuff matters most

One thing that really surprised me early on was that we all thought our initial proposition might be too simple to win: one platform to consolidate all payment methods (direct debits, cards, open banking) and automate credit control. There were already companies doing bits of this so we assumed most firms had this sorted.

We were wrong.

Every time we spoke to an accountant or bookkeeper, we kept hearing the same story: they were using multiple providers to get paid. GoCardless for direct debits. Stripe for cards. Something else for open banking. And none of them talked to each other. Multiple reports. Clunky workflows. Payment reminders that didn’t adapt to client behaviour. It wasn’t efficient and it definitely wasn’t simple.

What did we learn?? Simplicity wins.

That’s what we’ve tried to build with Adfin: an all-in-one payment platform designed to simplify collections. One place to send and track invoices. One place to collect payments via card, direct debit, or open banking. One view of everything. No need to glue together tools or deal with inconsistent workflows.

Funny thing is, we really thought this idea might be too basic. But when you see the pain clients go through to get things together, you realise how much value there is in just making things work properly. So even if your idea feels simple, if you’re confident there’s a real pain and you think you can fix it, build something quick and put it in front of people. You’ll learn fast either way.

‍

Why I enjoy working with accountants and bookkeepers

Something I’ve come to really appreciate over the past year is just how nice accountants and bookkeepers are as people, although they’re straight-talkers. If it’s cr*p, they’ll tell you. But if it works and they can see the value, they’ll back you, and they’ll tell others.

They genuinely care about their clients. They’re not just ticking boxes or moving numbers around. Most of the people I’ve spoken to want their clients to succeed, and they know that getting paid properly is a big part of that.

They also value the basics: trust, support, reliability. It’s not about nice product features or complex setups. If something works, is simple, and you’re there when they need help, that’s what earns their trust.

And the impact of that trust is real. Word of mouth actually works in this space. When someone loves what you’ve built, they’ll tell others. And if they don’t… well, you’ll hear about that too 🙂

We’re already seeing this in the number of firms switching over from other direct debit providers. Not because those products don’t work, but because they feel forgotten by them. Cheeky pricing, slow or non-existent support, worse payout terms, and a general sense that no one’s listening. I know it sounds cliché, but we’re really trying to do the opposite: put our customers first, offer great customer support (I recommend reading Chris’s post on how we run support), and stay honest from day one.

‍

Still early, still learning

We’re still early. The product’s better than it was, the team is stronger, and our customer base is growing, but there’s a lot more to build. More conversations to have. More trust to earn.

Looking back, the biggest shift for me this year wasn’t in how I pitched Adfin, but in how I understood the people we’re building for. What they deal with every day. What frustrates them. What matters to them when they choose a product and a company.

If you’re in the space and want to share your experience, I’d love to hear it. And if you’ve ever jumped on a call, given feedback, or told someone else about Adfin, thank you deeply.

We’ll keep showing up, listening, and improving. That’s the plan.

Name: Strategies for automating credit control processes
Post Body:
Why manual credit control is holding your business back

Credit control has always been essential to healthy cash flow, yet many businesses still treat it as a manual, reactive task. Finance teams chase overdue invoices one by one, track disputes in spreadsheets, and make credit decisions based on gut feeling rather than data. The result? Slower collections, higher bad debt, and teams stretched too thin to focus on growth.

Automating credit control processes isn't simply about sending reminders faster. It's a strategic shift that connects credit risk assessment, payment follow-ups, and dispute resolution into a single, intelligent workflow. For small and mid-sized businesses especially, this shift can mean the difference between predictable cash flow and constant financial firefighting.

Consider the scale of the problem: a 2025 study found that 98% of companies still rely on some manual processes in payment operations, with more than half indicating that between 26% and 50% of their payment operations are handled manually (CFO Tech). That's an enormous amount of time lost to repetitive tasks that automation handles in seconds.

What is automated credit control and why does it matter?

Automated credit control refers to the end-to-end automation of workflows that govern how a business extends credit, collects payments, and resolves disputes. It goes well beyond basic invoicing. A fully automated system covers credit risk scoring at the point of onboarding, dynamic payment reminder sequences, real-time reconciliation, and structured dispute management, all connected in a single process.

This matters because disconnected tools create gaps. If your invoicing system doesn't talk to your credit risk data, or your dispute tracker lives in a separate spreadsheet, information falls through the cracks. Automated credit control closes those gaps by creating a continuous loop: assess risk, send the invoice, chase payment through the right channels, flag disputes early, and reconcile once payment lands.

The business case is compelling. Companies relying on manual accounts receivable processes see their DSO stretch an average of 30% longer than automated ones (Zone & Co). For a business with standard 28-day credit terms, that gap can translate to weeks of delayed cash, directly affecting your ability to pay suppliers, invest, or hire.

How can you automate payment follow-ups and dispute management?

Structuring automated payment chasing workflows

Effective payment chasing isn't about sending more emails. It's about sending the right message, through the right channel, at the right time. Automated workflows allow you to build escalation sequences that adapt based on customer behaviour and risk profiles.

A typical automated chasing workflow might look like this:

  1. A polite reminder sent three days before the due date via email

  2. A follow-up on the day payment is due, including a direct payment link

  3. A firmer reminder at seven days overdue, sent via email and SMS

  4. An escalation at 14 days, potentially involving a phone call or WhatsApp message

  5. A final notice at 30 days, referencing late payment terms and next steps

The key advantage is consistency. Manual chasing is prone to missed follow-ups and inconsistent tone. Automated sequences ensure every customer receives timely, professional communication without your team lifting a finger. Platforms like Adfin enable businesses to automate payment chasing across multiple channels, including email, WhatsApp, and SMS, while syncing with accounting software to stop reminders the moment payment is received.

Timing matters enormously. Research shows that first contact within 48 hours of a missed payment achieves a 65% collection success rate, while waiting 14 days drops that rate to just 15% (Credit Pulse). Automation ensures you never miss that critical early window.

Integrating dispute management into the automation loop

Disputes are a hidden bottleneck in credit control. When a customer queries an invoice, the clock stops on payment. If that dispute sits unresolved in someone's inbox for two weeks, you've effectively extended your payment terms by 14 days without agreeing to it.

Automated dispute management solves this by routing queries to the right person immediately, tracking resolution timelines, and escalating stalled cases. The best systems categorise disputes by type, whether it's a pricing discrepancy, delivery issue, or duplicate invoice, and apply resolution workflows accordingly.

This matters more than most businesses realise. Businesses spend about 62% of their accounts receivable time on customer engagement tasks such as reminders and follow-ups (Resolve Pay). By automating the routine elements, your team can focus on resolving genuine disputes rather than chasing straightforward payments.

What should you look for in automated credit control tools?

AI-driven vs. rules-based approaches

Most credit control platforms fall into one of two camps: rules-based systems that follow predefined logic, or AI-driven tools that learn and adapt. The most effective approach combines both.

Rules-based engines are excellent for compliance guardrails and standard workflows. They ensure every customer receives the correct sequence of reminders based on invoice age, value, and payment terms. They're predictable, auditable, and easy to configure.

AI adds a layer of intelligence on top. Machine learning models can predict which customers are likely to pay late, recommend optimal contact times, and prioritise high-risk accounts for your collectors. Over time, the system learns from payment patterns and adjusts its strategies accordingly.

A hybrid approach gives you the best of both worlds: consistent processes where you need them, and adaptive intelligence where it makes the biggest difference.

Key capabilities that reduce DSO

When evaluating credit control tools, focus on capabilities that directly impact your days sales outstanding:

  • Real-time credit scoring that assesses customer risk before you extend terms

  • Multi-channel payment reminders that reach customers where they're most responsive

  • Self-service payment portals where customers can view invoices and pay instantly

  • Automated reconciliation that matches payments to invoices without manual intervention

  • Accounting software integration with platforms like Xero and QuickBooks for seamless data sync

Organisations that have implemented dedicated AR automation for over 50% of their operations have experienced a 32% decrease in DSO, equivalent to a reduction of 19 days (Invensis). That's cash arriving nearly three weeks sooner, a transformative improvement for any growing business.

How do you build a phased automation roadmap?

Jumping straight to full automation can overwhelm teams and systems. A phased approach delivers quick wins while building toward comprehensive transformation.

Phase 1: Quick wins (weeks 1-4). Start by automating payment reminders and integrating your invoicing with your accounting software. This alone eliminates the most repetitive manual work. Solutions like Adfin make this straightforward, offering automated chasing, multiple payment methods, and direct integration with Xero and QuickBooks, all without monthly fees.

Phase 2: Dispute and risk workflows (months 2-3). Introduce automated dispute routing and basic credit risk scoring. Categorise customers by payment behaviour and apply different chasing strategies to each segment. This is where you start seeing meaningful DSO improvements.

Phase 3: AI-driven optimisation (months 4-6). Layer in predictive analytics to forecast late payments, optimise contact timing, and continuously refine your collection strategies. At this stage, your system is learning from every interaction and improving autonomously.

Change management matters just as much as the technology. Upskill your AR team to interpret dashboards, handle escalations, and manage the exceptions that automation surfaces. The goal isn't to replace people but to redirect their expertise toward higher-value work.

The results speak for themselves. Nearly 91% of mid-sized firms with fully automated AR systems report increased savings, cash flow, and growth (Upflow). Yet nearly half of finance teams have automated only a few AR tasks, with over a third still relying entirely on manual processes. The opportunity gap is significant.

Meanwhile, the cost of inaction continues to mount. Most businesses offer 28-day credit terms, but average DSO sits at 67 days, and businesses in the Americas lose 51.9% of unpaid receivables not paid within 90 days (Sage). Automation directly addresses this by compressing the collection cycle and flagging at-risk accounts before debts become uncollectible. In fact, businesses using AR automation typically see a 10-15% drop in bad debt write-offs, as automated workflows help teams flag at-risk accounts early.

FAQs

Which types of tools handle both payment follow-ups and disputes?

Look for end-to-end accounts receivable platforms that combine automated chasing with dispute tracking and resolution workflows. Platforms like Adfin cover payment follow-ups across multiple channels while integrating with accounting software. For dispute management specifically, seek tools that offer case routing, escalation timelines, and root cause categorisation within the same system.

How quickly can automated credit control reduce days sales outstanding?

Most businesses see measurable improvements within the first 30 to 60 days of implementing automated payment reminders. Deeper reductions, particularly from dispute workflow automation and AI-driven prioritisation, typically emerge over three to six months as the system learns customer behaviour patterns and refines its approach.

Is automation suitable for small finance teams?

Absolutely. Small teams benefit the most because automation multiplies their capacity without adding headcount. A single person can manage hundreds of accounts when reminders, reconciliation, and escalations run automatically. Many modern platforms require no technical setup, integrating directly with existing accounting software.

Will automated reminders damage customer relationships?

Not when done correctly. The best systems send personalised messages that appear to come directly from your team, maintaining your brand's tone and professionalism. Automated workflows can include thank-you messages after payment, further strengthening relationships rather than straining them.

What payment methods should an automated credit control system support?

Flexibility is key. Look for platforms that support cards, direct debits, open banking, and traditional bank transfers. Offering customers their preferred payment method removes friction and accelerates collection. Adfin, for example, supports all of these methods, ensuring customers can pay however suits them best.

How does automation handle exceptions and edge cases?

Good automation systems are designed to flag exceptions rather than ignore them. Partial payments, disputed amounts, and unusual payment patterns get routed to your team for human review, while routine collections continue running in the background. This ensures nothing falls through the cracks without burdening your team with every transaction.

Do I need to replace my accounting software to automate credit control?

No. Most modern credit control platforms integrate with popular accounting tools like Xero, QuickBooks, and Sage. The automation layer sits on top of your existing system, pulling invoice data and syncing payment status in real time without requiring a full technology overhaul.

Name: Taking a leap: Jim’s journey to building a client-first firm
Post Body:
"With Adfin, clients don’t really get the option to delay because it’s so seamless. When clients started saying, “Wow, that was so easy to pay,” I knew we were onto something."

In the spotlight this week is Jim, the founder of his own growing accountancy practice. Jim talks about taking the leap from a 14-year career to self-employment with a newborn at home, why small businesses and start-ups are his sweet spot, and how Adfin got his clients saying “Wow, that was so easy to pay”.

How did you get into accounting and start your business? How did you get to where you are now?

I actually started in accounting through school work experience - I did two weeks at an accounting firm and then stayed there for the next 14 years. So I was kind of stuck in one place for a long time.

Eventually, I just outgrew it. I got fully qualified, built strong relationships with clients, and it naturally progressed to me going out on my own. A few clients put their trust in me and said they’d come along, so one day I went home, told my wife, “I’ve quit,” and that was that. We had an eight-week-old baby at home at the time too, so it was a bit of a whirlwind.

Since then, it’s really grown. We've prioritised service, built client relationships - even just through social media - and it’s made a big difference. My wife joined the business in January, we moved into our new office in June, and our first employee started this month. It’s all happened so fast.

What memorable experience from work sticks in your mind?

Me and a few colleagues were in a hotel to attend a conference down in London and over dinner one of them asked ‘Where is the pool?’ We thought he was joking or referencing a pool table. NOPE, he meant swimming pool.

He also revealed he had packed his swimming shorts…we were staying in a Premier Inn. History was made.

Did you face any big challenges or surprises going from employment to running your own practice?

Definitely the admin. I didn’t realise just how much time you spend behind the scenes. When I was employed, I thought I’d just churn out work all day, but when you’re running things, your inbox is full of stuff from your governing body, insurance, new software - you name it. It’s a juggle to balance admin and billable work.

‍Do you specialise or work with any specific clients?

I’ve stuck to what I know best: smaller businesses and people just starting out. Especially after going through that journey myself, I now see what those clients went through. I love supporting sole traders and new business owners because they often become your bigger clients down the line.

It’s great working with people from day one because you can set them up the right way instead of correcting old habits. They want to be led, they listen to advice, and it makes the job easier and more rewarding.

If you could have a dream client at the click of your fingers, who would that be?

Honestly, a little café. I’ve always wanted to work with one. They’ve got everything - cash, card, tills, staff - all within four walls. Even though they’re small, they need quite a lot of support, which I find really interesting and feel I can be a big help to them.

I think I’ve spent so much time working in cafés over the past year (before we got the new office) that it’s just become a bit of a dream. 

Do you have any fun or interesting stories from your journey so far?

There are loads, honestly. Me and my wife have a running joke - whenever something big happens, I’ll come downstairs and say, “This is the turning point.” I probably said that every couple of weeks for a while.

Whether it was signing a new client, signing for our office, upgrading the computer, or the first time we took a wage - it all felt like a major moment. We laugh about it now, but those little moments really marked the growth.

‍Are there any tech trends you’re excited about?

We're on Engager, so for me, it’s the integrations. I love that I don’t have to duplicate information anymore. It’s not about learning loads of new software - it’s about how well everything connects behind the scenes.

That’s one thing I love about Adfin too. I don’t need to update client emails in multiple systems - it just flows. It used to feel like software companies were all competing, but now there’s more collaboration and it’s made life so much easier.

Before Adfin, how did you manage getting paid?

We were using GoCardless and also just sending invoices, hoping clients would grab the bank details and pay. But that process had friction. People would open the email on their phone, think, “I’ll deal with this later,” and forget.

That’s where Adfin helped - clients don’t really get the option to delay because it’s so seamless. It just happens.

Everything feeds into the customer experience. We’re a service-driven business, so if paying us is easy, that reflects well.

When clients started saying, “Wow, that was so easy to pay,” I knew we were onto something. It’s made a difference in getting paid faster too - we send tax returns and payments together, instead of waiting weeks between them.

What’s your favourite feature on Adfin?

Apple Pay, without a doubt. Those invoices get paid instantly. It’s just easy - the way the email looks, how simple it is to click and pay - it’s a winner.

What’s your go to drink when you’re off the clock?

Cider - fruity ones like Kopparberg. If I walk into a pub and they’ve got strawberry and lime Rekorderlig on tap, that’s my go-to.

What’s one task you love doing, and one you’d happily never do again?

I absolutely love mowing the grass. When you’ve got a young kid, it’s the perfect excuse to go outside for 20 minutes and block everything out. I tell them, “You can’t come out - it’s dangerous!”

The task I’d never do again? Washing up. I can’t stand it. We don’t have a dishwasher, so it’s just gross. I’m fine with drying and putting things away, but touching food on plates? No thanks. If I ever win something in a raffle, I hope it’s a dishwasher.

If you could automate anything in your life, what would it be?

Tracking my mileage. I know there are a million apps out there, but I wish it was built into my car - just press a button when I start the engine and it logs everything.

I tell clients to track mileage all the time, but when I have to do it myself, I totally get why it’s a pain. You have to remember, turn on GPS, log the trip - it’s just not a habit yet. If Tesla hasn’t already done that, they need to!

If you weren’t an accountant, what would you have been?

I originally applied for my work experience with an electrician. I enjoyed maths mainly due to the clear line of right & wrong answers and thought being an electrician would be similar (it works or it doesn’t). Sadly, apparently being colour blind is a limiting factor in such a trade, so due to safety concerns, I fell at the first hurdle - I imagine getting the wiring colours right is very important!
